**Authors:** Brian Holzman, Jeehee Han, Bethany Lewis, and Irina Chukhray
**Source:** AERA Open, Volume 12 (2026), pp. 1–20. DOI: 10.1177/23328584261467394
**Review Date:** 2026-09-02

### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

This is a large-N (1,366,603 bachelor's-only workers aged 25–64), publicly replicable descriptive study that crosses two established measures — DiPrete et al.'s (2017) major–occupation linkage index and Bol et al.'s (2019) match indicator — with race, nativity, and immigrant-destination state type in the 2013–2017 ACS. The field can rely on what it documents: working in a matched occupation is associated with roughly 16–23% higher annual earnings in every racial group; that premium is larger for foreign-born than U.S.-born workers within every group; stronger-linkage majors are associated with lower odds of (short-spell) unemployment; and immigrants of every race sort into higher-linkage majors yet have about half the odds of working in a matched occupation. What the paper does not establish is its most quotable claim — that alignment makes racial and nativity disparities smaller. Every outcome model is estimated separately by race, so no between-group gap is ever estimated or tested; the "benefit more" narrative rests on an eyeballed 2–3 log-point difference in one interaction term (Linkage × Match: .039 White, .060 Black, .069 Hispanic, .041 Asian) across separately fitted models, applies only to the ~16% of workers who are matched, and is absent for Asian workers. Several execution issues compound this: the abstract and introduction assert a linkage–earnings association that Table 3 and the paper's own Results text contradict; the Foreign Born coefficients (−.29 to −.64) are at-arrival intercepts (years in the U.S. is a covariate) yet are narrated as the immigrant penalty; annual earnings are modeled with no hours or weeks controls; linkage inference never clusters on the 36 majors that define the regressor; and Appendix Table A1's headers contradict the stated match-construction rule in a way that, if real, would mechanically steepen the headline interaction. All five sub-reviews independently rated the paper adequate. Read it as a well-documented benchmark of conditional associations, cite it for the match premium and the alignment profile by race and nativity, and attach explicit caveats to anything about gaps, immigrant penalty magnitudes, destination-context heterogeneity, or policy.

#### Key Strengths

- Scale and verifiability: 1.37 million public IPUMS ACS observations, a deposited openICPSR replication package (10.3886/E249905V1), open-access supplements, and — unusually — full publication of both constructed measures (Figure A1 gives all 36 linkage scores; Table A1 gives the complete matched-occupation crosswalk), so the measure-construction stage can be independently checked. Sample partitions reconcile to the person across Tables 3, 5, and 6.
- Consistent, prominent causal restraint. "Descriptive associations" appears in the abstract, introduction, methods, and a free-standing Limitations section that argues the direction of likely bias (selection into high-linkage majors biases the linkage association toward zero; selection into matched jobs biases the match association upward). The robustness program — 170-category linkage with 36-field fixed effects, Census-region and -division linkage measures, LPM analogues, and re-estimation on perfect-prediction-reduced samples — is more than perfunctory.
- The occupational match premium (.155–.229 log points, p < .001 in every racial group and nearly every destination cell) and the consistently positive Match × Foreign Born term (.078–.176) are well-powered, stable across every reported specification, and constitute the paper's best citable outputs.
- It fills a real gap between Bol et al. (2019), who linked alignment to outcomes but pooled across groups, and Lu et al. (2024), who documented racial differences in linkage but not their consequences. The immigrant-destination stratification is an original move that shows pooled national estimates hide sign reversals (e.g., Hispanic and Asian match odds above White in established destinations but below in nondestinations).
- Table notes are complete and self-contained (estimator, weights, fixed effects, covariate list, reference categories, odds-ratio reporting), and sample drops are documented exactly (footnotes 7, 10, 11).

#### Key Concerns

- The headline claim that racial and nativity disparities are "smaller" among aligned workers is never estimated. All earnings and unemployment models are race-stratified (Tables 3, 4, 6, 7); there is no pooled model with race × alignment interactions and no formal cross-group test. The "benefit more" reading rests on informal comparison of Linkage × Match across separately fitted models, and the Asian coefficient (.041) is indistinguishable from White (.039).
- The summarizing prose diverges from the tables in exactly the sentences most likely to be quoted: the Introduction says Hispanic workers choose stronger-linkage majors when Table 2 (col. 1) shows −.011; the abstract says linkage is associated with higher earnings when all four Table 3 main effects are zero or negative and the Results text says so; the "3.9%" figure for matched White workers is the interaction coefficient rather than the marginal effect (−.008 + .039 = 3.1%); and interaction terms are repeatedly narrated as total group effects (e.g., Hispanic immigrants vs. Hispanic natives on linkage is +.207 − .028 = +.18, not "weaker").
- The Foreign Born main effects (−.292 to −.642 log points; unemployment ORs up to 4.5–4.8) are evaluated at zero years in the United States because years-in-U.S. and its square are covariates that are zero for natives — while the average immigrant in the sample has been in the country 20 years. The paper never states this, narrates the coefficients as the immigrant penalty, and builds its "match offsets the immigrant disadvantage" arithmetic against that at-arrival intercept.
- Measurement and inference problems bear directly on the headline interaction: Table A1 is headed "Most Common Occupation" and its low-linkage entries (liberal arts and ethnic studies → secretaries; history → retail supervisors; philosophy → retail salespersons) look frequency-ranked rather than ratio-ranked as the Method states, which would depress match premia for low-linkage majors and steepen Linkage × Match by construction; annual earnings are modeled without hours, weeks, or full-time controls, so match premia (especially Match × Foreign Born) mix wage and labor-supply margins; linkage takes only 36 values and is never clustered at the major level, so reported SEs on every linkage term are too small; and the linkage variable is severely right-skewed with its tail occupied by small-cell majors (≥100-observation floor, no bias correction).

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The rows of Table A1 follow the stated ratio rule; the header is the mislabel. In the openICPSR deposit (10.3886/E249905V1), RaceNativityLabor_TabA1.do keeps the top two occupations by an adjusted rank built from the actual-to-counterfactual ratio, and the deposited rank correlates 0.99 with a ratio ranking and 0.27 with raw frequency within majors. The concern that the match variable was built on frequency for low-linkage majors, which would bias Linkage × Match upward, does not hold (moderate confidence: the top-two sets only partly reproduce). Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the ICPSR deposit.

- The destination-heterogeneity narrative and the policy recommendations (steer minorities toward high-linkage majors; extend 60×30TX; target immigrant-destination states) rest on the thinnest evidence in the paper: roughly 160 untested comparisons across Tables 5–7, nondestination cells of 2,372–5,763 observations, two Table 7 models whose goodness-of-fit statistics (1987.955, 25.422) indicate failure to fit, and a static state classification with undisclosed operationalization. Linkage alone carries no earnings return, and the groups the policy would target are the ones least likely to achieve the match on which the return depends. The literature review also omits the horizontal-mismatch economics (Robst 2007; Altonji et al.), the immigrant-selectivity literature that supplies the leading alternative explanation for the nativity results, and the licensing–wage-gap work (Blair & Chung 2019) that anticipates the paper's mechanism.

#### What to Rely On

- The occupational match earnings premium among U.S. bachelor's-only workers: roughly .16–.23 log points in every racial group (Table 3), stable across LPM, regional-linkage, and 170-category specifications. Read it as a return to being in a matched job (annual earnings, no hours control), not a wage-rate return.
- The match premium is larger for foreign-born than U.S.-born workers within every racial group (Match × Foreign Born .078–.176, all p < .001). The interaction is unaffected by the years-in-U.S. parameterization problem that afflicts the Foreign Born main effect.
- The alignment profile by nativity (Table 2): immigrants of all races choose higher-linkage majors (+.21–.24 SD) but have roughly half the odds of working in a matched occupation (OR ≈ .50–.55). This is the paper's clearest advance over Lu et al. (2024).
- The alignment profile by race, read for magnitudes: Asian workers choose noticeably higher-linkage majors (+.10 SD) and match more often (OR 1.15); Black workers choose slightly higher-linkage majors (+.04 SD) but match less often (OR .89); all non-Asian race differences are under a tenth of a standard deviation (R² = .021). Do not cite this as evidence of large racial differences in alignment.
- Linkage alone has no positive association with earnings (Table 3 main effects −.008, .000, −.001, .012); the earnings return to linkage exists only conditional on match (Linkage × Match .039–.069). This is the correct one-line summary of Table 3, and it is the paper's Results text — not its abstract — that states it.
- Stronger-linkage majors are associated with lower odds of unemployment in all four groups (ORs .865–.930, Table 4), with the caveat that the sample is positive earners, so this is short-spell unemployment among people who worked in the prior year.
- The existence (not the magnitude) of destination-context heterogeneity: the sign of the Hispanic and Asian match differential relative to White workers flips between established-destination and nondestination states (Table 5, cols. 4 and 6).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "Racial and nativity differences in earnings and unemployment are smaller among individuals with majors tied to specific occupations and who work in jobs related to their majors" (abstract) — no between-group gap is estimated anywhere; every outcome model is race-stratified and no cross-group test is reported.
- "Black, Hispanic, and foreign-born workers appear to benefit more from major–occupation alignment" — the differential is a 2–3 log-point difference in Linkage × Match across separately fitted models (informal t ≈ 2.3 and 2.9), never formally tested, applies only to the ~16% of workers who are matched, and is absent for Asian workers (.041 vs. .039); the Results text's generalization to "racial and ethnic minorities" is too broad.
- Any magnitude of the immigrant earnings penalty (Foreign Born −.29 to −.64) or the unemployment odds ratios of 4.5–4.8 — these are intercept shifts at zero years in the U.S.; the years-in-U.S. coefficients are not reported, so the gap for a typical (20-year) immigrant cannot be recovered from the paper.
- The "3.9% higher earnings" figure for matched White workers — the marginal effect is Linkage + Linkage × Match = −.008 + .039 = 3.1%; the comparison figures for Black (6.0%) and Hispanic (6.8%, not 6.9%) should be computed the same way.
- The Introduction's statement that Hispanic workers choose stronger-linkage majors — Table 2 col. 1 is −.011 (p < .05); and the sign depends on nativity: U.S.-born Hispanic workers are at +.012 while the pooled negative is driven by Hispanic immigrants (Hispanic × Foreign Born −.028). Cite the table cell, not the summary sentence.
- Any sentence saying a group of immigrants is "more" or "less" likely to do something — check whether it describes an interaction coefficient or a total effect. Hispanic immigrants choose higher-linkage majors than Hispanic natives (+.207 − .028), and Asian immigrants have lower match odds than Asian natives (.535 × 1.298 ≈ .69), contrary to the prose in places.
- The match premium as a wage-rate return, and especially Match × Foreign Born — annual earnings with no hours, weeks, or full-time control; differential part-time/part-year work among unmatched immigrants would produce the same pattern with no wage difference.
- The precision of every linkage coefficient (Linkage, Linkage × Match, Linkage × Foreign Born, three-way terms) — the regressor takes 36 values and is not clustered at the major level; treat marginal (+ and single-star) linkage results as null.
- The Linkage × Match interaction itself pending a check of Table A1 against Equations 2–3 in the openICPSR deposit — if match was built on frequency for low-linkage majors, the interaction is biased upward by construction.
- "One standard deviation of linkage" as a counterfactual — the distribution is bounded near −1 SD with a thin tail to +5 SD occupied by a few small vocational majors (nuclear technologies, cosmetology/culinary arts), and the standardization convention is not stated; the units of every headline magnitude are provisional.
- Everything in the nondestination columns of Tables 6 and 7 (N = 2,372–5,763; Hispanic Linkage × Match .260 and Match × Foreign Born .527; Asian Linkage OR .176 with Linkage × Foreign Born 5.942; goodness-of-fit 1987.955 and 25.422) — the paper cautions only about the Asian cell; neither should inform any conclusion.
- The destination-context policy recommendation and mechanism claims (networks, receptivity, state policy) — no cross-context equality tests, ~160 unadjusted comparisons, a classification that is 'six big states vs. 26 states + DC vs. the rest' confounded with region and urbanicity, and no mechanism measured.
- The recommendation to steer minority and immigrant students toward high-linkage majors — linkage alone carries no earnings return; the return requires match, which is precisely the step where these groups fall behind; no lever affecting match is identified, and alignment premia are equilibrium prices.
- The unemployment results as evidence about labor-force attachment — the sample is restricted to positive earners (2.0% unemployment rate), removing the long-term unemployed a mismatch story would most implicate.
- The novelty claim ("the first to do so by race and nativity") — narrowly true for the DiPrete/Bol measures, but major–job mismatch returns by race and nativity have been studied in labor economics (Robst 2007; Xu 2013) and the immigrant overeducation/brain-waste literature (Beckhusen et al. 2013; Mattoo et al. 2008; Chiswick & Miller).
- Interpretations attributing immigrant patterns to discrimination, closure, or networks — the immigrant educational-selectivity literature (Feliciano 2005; Hamilton 2014/2019; Lee & Zhou 2015) predicts the same patterns compositionally and is never engaged; nothing in the covariates proxies pre-migration selection. "Foreign born" also pools foreign-educated with U.S.-educated (1.5-generation) immigrants, whose credential-recognition situations differ sharply.
- The paper's account of Lu et al. (2024) — it reports Lu et al. finding weaker linkage among Black graduates, then finds the opposite (+.042) without reconciling the two; check sample definitions (this paper is bachelor's-highest only) before citing either.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

A competent, transparent, large-N descriptive study that uses well-established measures (DiPrete et al.'s mutual-information linkage index; Bol et al.'s match indicator) on 1.37 million ACS respondents, is candid that its estimates are associations rather than effects, and deposits data and code publicly. But the execution has several issues that matter for exactly the claims the abstract makes: annual earnings are modeled without any labor-supply control, the Foreign Born coefficient is evaluated at zero years in the United States yet is narrated throughout as the immigrant earnings gap, Appendix Table A1 contradicts the stated rule for constructing the match variable, standard errors on the key linkage regressor ignore that it takes only 36 values, and the racial/nativity 'smaller disparities' headline is never actually estimated anywhere in the paper. Rely on the broad descriptive patterns; treat the differential-returns and destination-heterogeneity claims as suggestive.

**Strengths:**

- Measurement is anchored in two well-vetted published constructions (DiPrete et al. 2017 mutual-information linkage; Bol et al. 2019 actual/counterfactual match ratio) rather than invented ad hoc, so results are comparable to an existing literature, and the departures from DiPrete et al. are disclosed and justified (footnote 6: majors are only reported for bachelor's degrees in ACS, so education is held constant and the attainment term drops out).
- The paper is repeatedly and correctly explicit that estimates are descriptive: the Method section, the Limitations section, and the Discussion all state this, and the Limitations section reasons about the *direction* of likely bias (selection into high-linkage majors by marginalized students biases the linkage-earnings association toward zero; selection into matched jobs biases the match-earnings association upward). That is better practice than the usual boilerplate disclaimer.
- Sample size and precision are genuine assets for the pooled analyses. Table 2 (N = 1,366,603) and Table 3's White (N = 1,055,143), Black (90,350), Hispanic (106,122), and Asian (114,988) subsamples support tight estimates of the central associations; the Match coefficients in Table 3 (.155 to .229 log points, SEs .003 to .018) are estimated far more precisely than most of this literature manages.
- Survey design is respected in the mechanics: ACS person weights are applied throughout, standard errors use Taylor-linearized variance estimation accounting for stratification and clustering, and state and year fixed effects absorb geographic and temporal variation in labor markets — a real improvement on Bol et al. (2019) and Lu et al. (2024), which pool nationally.
- An unusually thorough robustness apparatus is reported in the online supplement: LPM analogues for every logit (Tables OA1-OA4), linkage and match measures rebuilt within Census regions (OB1-OB7) and divisions (OC1-OC7), and a 170-category field-of-study reconstruction with 36 broad-field fixed effects added (OD1-OD7). Footnotes 10 and 11 also report re-estimating the earnings models on the reduced samples created by perfect prediction in the unemployment logits.
- Data and analysis files are deposited at openICPSR (doi 10.3886/E249905V1), so the construction choices flagged below are, in principle, checkable by readers rather than matters of faith.

**Weaknesses:**

- No labor-supply control in the earnings models. The dependent variable is log *annual* earnings, and the covariate list — spelled out identically in the notes to Tables 2, 3, 5, 6 — contains age, age squared, gender, years in the U.S. and its square, native-English-speaker status, disability, marital status, number of children, and metro-mix/nonmetro indicators. There are no hours, no weeks worked, no full-time/part-year indicator, and no occupation or industry controls. The linkage *measure* was built on full-time, non-self-employed workers (Method, p. 5), but the regression sample is anyone with positive earnings. So the Match premium in Table 3 (.155 to .229) is a mix of a wage return and a labor-supply margin, and the Match x Foreign Born coefficients (.084 to .176) inherit the same ambiguity: if immigrants in unmatched jobs are disproportionately part-time or part-year, that alone produces a larger match 'premium' for immigrants with no wage difference at all.
- The Foreign Born main effect is not the immigrant-native gap. Because years-in-U.S. and years-in-U.S.-squared are covariates that are structurally zero for the native-born, the Foreign Born coefficient is evaluated at zero years in the country — a hypothetical just-arrived immigrant. Table 1 reports mean years in the U.S. among the foreign-born of 20.5 (23.1 White, 19.9 Black, 20.6 Hispanic, 18.9 Asian). The years-in-U.S. coefficients are never reported, so readers cannot recover the gap for a typical immigrant. Yet the text narrates these coefficients as levels throughout: 'Foreign-born individuals face a disadvantage, with their earnings substantially lower' (Table 3: -.292, -.607, -.642, -.356), and the Discussion's arithmetic about match premiums 'offsetting' the disadvantage compares a real interaction against an at-arrival intercept shift. The same problem produces the odd Table 7 White-nondestination Foreign Born odds ratio of 4.462 (SE 1.872) and the Asian-nondestination 4.843 (SE 5.164).
- Appendix Table A1 contradicts the stated match rule. The Method (p. 5) says occupations are ranked by the ratio of actual to counterfactual frequency and the top two are the matched occupations. But Table A1's column headers read 'Most Common Occupation' and 'Second Most Common Occupation,' and the entries for weak-linkage majors look frequency-based, not ratio-based: ethnic studies matches to 'Secretaries & administrative assistants' and 'Human resource workers'; liberal arts to 'Secretaries & administrative assistants' and 'Elementary & middle school teachers'; history to 'Secondary school teachers' and 'First-line supervisors of retail sales workers'; philosophy/religion to 'Clergy' and 'Retail salespersons.' Under a ratio rule, economy-wide-common occupations carry large counterfactual denominators and should almost never top the ranking; secretaries and retail salespersons topping two and appearing in two more is very hard to reconcile with Equations 2-3. Either the labels are wrong or the variable was built on frequency for at least some majors — and if the latter, the effect falls disproportionately on low-linkage majors, mechanically depressing their match premium and inflating the Linkage x Match interaction that is the paper's headline coefficient.
- Standard errors on the linkage terms ignore the 36-cluster structure of the regressor. Linkage takes exactly 36 values (one per ACS major category); the Taylor-linearized variance estimator handles ACS strata and household clustering, but nothing in the paper clusters at the major level. This is a textbook Moulton setting, and the affected coefficients are the ones the paper leans on: Linkage, Linkage x Match, Linkage x Foreign Born, and the three-way term, in Tables 3, 4, 6 and 7. With effectively 36 clusters, the true sampling variability of these terms is larger — plausibly substantially larger — than the reported SEs of .001 to .014 imply.
- The linkage variable is severely right-skewed and its tail is confounded with major size. Figure A1 shows all 36 majors between roughly -0.9 and +5.0 standardized units: the KL-divergence construction is bounded below at zero and unbounded above, so the mass of majors sits in a narrow band and a handful of small vocational fields (nuclear technologies ~+5, cosmetology/culinary arts ~+4.5, electrical/mechanical repairs ~+3.5, library science ~+3) sit far out. Two problems follow. First, in OLS these high-leverage majors disproportionately drive every linkage coefficient, and no leverage check or trimming analysis is reported. Second, plug-in estimators of mutual information are biased upward at small cell counts, and footnote 7 sets the inclusion threshold at only 100 observations per major — so small majors mechanically receive higher linkage scores, and the extreme tail is precisely where the smallest majors sit. The implausible cosmetology/culinary-arts match to 'Morticians, undertakers, & funeral directors' in Table A1 is the kind of artifact small cells produce. No bias correction (Miller-Madow, jackknife) is mentioned.
- The unemployment outcome is defined on a peculiar sample. The paper states that 'the unemployment analyses use the same analytic sample as the earnings analyses' (p. 8), and that sample is 'individuals reporting positive earnings in the survey year' (p. 6). So unemployment is measured among people who had positive earnings during the prior twelve months, which excludes the long-term unemployed and everyone out of the labor force with zero earnings. The resulting 2.0% unemployment rate (Table 1) is well below the actual 2013-2017 rate for BA holders. There is also a timing mismatch — earnings are last-12-months, employment status is at survey. Table 4 and Table 7 therefore describe short-spell unemployment conditional on having worked recently, not labor force attachment.
- The abstract's central claim is never estimated. All earnings and unemployment models are fit separately by race (Tables 3, 4, 6, 7), so no White-Black, White-Hispanic, or White-Asian gap coefficient appears anywhere in the paper, at any level of linkage or match. The claim that 'racial and nativity differences in earnings and unemployment are smaller among individuals with majors tied to specific occupations and who work in jobs related to their majors' is inferred by eyeballing separately-fitted Linkage x Match coefficients (.039 White, .060 Black, .069 Hispanic, .041 Asian) across four models with different intercepts and different covariate distributions. The cross-model differences are never formally tested, and no predicted gap is computed at any point in the linkage-match space.
- The heterogeneity narrative rests on a very large, unadjusted grid of tests with some cells that are visibly broken. Tables 5-7 together contain on the order of 160 focal coefficients with no multiplicity adjustment and no formal cross-subsample equality tests, and the destination story is assembled by reading significance stars across it. The nondestination cells are the thinnest and most fragile: Table 6 Hispanic nondestination has N = 2,756 with Match x Foreign Born = .527 (SE .135) and Linkage x Match = .260 (SE .072); Table 7 Asian nondestination reports a Linkage odds ratio of .176 (SE .114) and Linkage x Foreign Born of 5.942 (SE 4.038) on N = 2,372. The reported goodness-of-fit statistics in the two nondestination columns of Table 7 Panel B — 1987.955 for Hispanic and 25.422 for Asian, against values under 1.4 in every other column — indicate the models did not fit; the paper flags caution for the Asian nondestination cell but not the Hispanic one, and both feed the abstract's destination claim.
- The introduction misstates the paper's own result. On p. 2 the summary reads that 'workers who are Asian, Black, Hispanic, and foreign-born are more likely to complete a college major with a stronger linkage than workers who are White and U.S. born,' but Table 2 Column 1 gives Hispanic = -.011 (SE .005, p < .05), i.e. *lower* linkage — and the Results and Discussion sections both correctly say Hispanic workers choose weaker-linkage majors. Compounding this, the Hispanic linkage coefficient flips sign between Table 2 Column 1 (-.011) and Column 2 (+.012), because Column 2 conditions on nativity; the pooled negative comes entirely from Hispanic immigrants (Hispanic x Foreign Born = -.028).
- 'Foreign born' pools two groups the paper's own theory distinguishes. The occupational-closure and credential-transferability mechanisms invoked throughout apply to people who earned their degree abroad, not to 1.5-generation immigrants who arrived as children and hold a U.S. bachelor's. ACS carries year of immigration and age, so age at arrival is constructible, but the models use only a years-in-U.S. quadratic and never separate foreign-educated from U.S.-educated immigrants.
- The destination classification is not a clean immigrant-density gradient, and it involves undisclosed researcher choices. The 'new destination' category (26 states plus DC per footnote 4) holds more of the sample (N = 680,344) than the six 'established' states (564,888) and includes MA, MD, VA, WA, GA and NC; 'nondestination' is only 121,371 observations (8.9%) across roughly 18 mostly small, rural, low-cost states, confounded with region, urbanicity, and industry mix. The authors also add New Jersey to Massey and Capoferro's established list and AL, NM, OK and SC to the new-destination list, and include DC where the original excludes it (footnote 4), with no sensitivity analysis on those choices.
- Conditioning on 'bachelor's degree is the highest credential' is conditioning on a post-treatment outcome. Majors whose graduates typically continue to graduate school (biology to medicine, psychology to MSW, social science to law) are systematically underrepresented, and the composition of BA-only holders within a major almost certainly differs by race and nativity. Footnote 6 presents this only as a data constraint on measuring linkage, not as a selection issue for the outcome models.
- The match indicator is fixed at exactly two occupations per major regardless of major size or breadth, so 'matched' means something very different across majors — perhaps 40% of nursing graduates versus a few percent of liberal arts graduates. Combined with the fact that linkage and match are both functions of the same conditional distribution p(occupation | major) (weighted correlation .275, footnote 9; Figure A2 shows linkage is visibly higher for Match = 1), part of the Linkage x Match interaction is mechanical rather than behavioral.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat the Table 2 sorting results as the most reliable thing in the paper — but read the magnitudes, not the stars. With N = 1,366,603 essentially everything is significant; the adjusted differences are .042 SD (Black), -.011 SD (Hispanic), .100 SD (Asian), and the model R-squared is .021. The raw means in Table 1 tell the same story (-.015 White, .023 Black, -.004 Hispanic, .138 Asian). The honest summary is that only Asian workers sort into higher-linkage majors to any noticeable degree, and everyone else differs from White workers by well under a tenth of a standard deviation. Do not cite this paper as evidence of large racial differences in major-occupation alignment.
- Read every Foreign Born coefficient as 'immigrant at the moment of arrival,' not 'the average immigrant.' Table 3's -.292 / -.607 / -.642 / -.356 and Table 7's odds ratios of 4.462 and 4.843 are intercept shifts evaluated at years-in-U.S. = 0, while the sample mean is 20.5 years. Since the years-in-U.S. coefficients are not reported, the actual immigrant-native gap for a typical immigrant is not recoverable from the paper, and the Discussion's language about match premiums 'offsetting' the foreign-born disadvantage should not be read as a quantitative offset calculation. The interaction terms (Match x Foreign Born, Linkage x Foreign Born) are unaffected by this and remain interpretable as differentials.
- Read the Match coefficients in Tables 3 and 6 as returns to being in a matched *job*, not as returns to a matched *wage rate*. With annual earnings as the outcome and no hours, weeks, or full-time control anywhere in the specification, a nontrivial share of the 15%-to-23% match premium is likely labor supply. This caveat applies with particular force to the Match x Foreign Born terms, since employment intensity differs sharply by nativity. If you need a wage-rate interpretation, verify against the deposited data before citing.
- Before building on the Linkage x Match interaction — the paper's single most load-bearing coefficient — check Appendix Table A1 against Equations 2-3 yourself. The listed matches for ethnic studies, liberal arts, history and philosophy/religion (secretaries, retail supervisors, retail salespersons) look frequency-ranked rather than ratio-ranked, contrary to the stated method, and if the match variable was in fact built on frequency for low-linkage majors, the Linkage x Match interaction is biased upward by construction. The openICPSR deposit (doi 10.3886/E249905V1) makes this checkable.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The rows of Table A1 follow the stated ratio rule; the header is the mislabel. In the openICPSR deposit (10.3886/E249905V1), RaceNativityLabor_TabA1.do keeps the top two occupations by an adjusted rank built from the actual-to-counterfactual ratio, and the deposited rank correlates 0.99 with a ratio ranking and 0.27 with raw frequency within majors. The concern that the match variable was built on frequency for low-linkage majors, which would bias Linkage × Match upward, does not hold (moderate confidence: the top-two sets only partly reproduce). Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the ICPSR deposit.

- Discount the precision of every linkage coefficient. Linkage takes only 36 distinct values and is not clustered at the major level, so reported SEs of .001 to .014 on Linkage, Linkage x Match, and Linkage x Foreign Born understate true uncertainty. Marginal results — such as the Linkage x Foreign Born term in Table 4 (1.067, p < .10 for White workers) — should be treated as null.
- Treat linkage as a coarse, tail-driven index rather than a continuous dose. Figure A1 shows a floor near -0.9 SD and a tail out to +5 SD occupied by a few small vocational fields (nuclear technologies, cosmetology/culinary arts, electrical/mechanical repairs, library science). A 'one standard deviation increase in linkage' is not a realistic counterfactual for most graduates, and the coefficients are disproportionately identified off those few extreme majors — which, given the 100-observation inclusion floor (footnote 7) and the upward small-sample bias of plug-in mutual-information estimators, are also the majors whose linkage scores are least trustworthy.
- Do not cite the abstract's 'disparities are smaller among matched workers' conclusion as an estimated result. No race gap is estimated anywhere in the paper; the models are race-stratified. The defensible version of the finding is narrower: the Linkage x Match coefficient is larger for Black (.060) and Hispanic (.069) than for White (.039) workers, with informal differences of roughly 2.3 and 2.9 standard errors that the paper never formally tests — and the Asian coefficient (.041) is indistinguishable from White. Note also that the text's '3.9% higher earnings' for White matched workers is the interaction term alone; the total is -.008 + .039 = 3.1%.
- Use Tables 5-7 as exploratory. Roughly 160 focal coefficients across three tables, no multiplicity adjustment, no formal tests of whether coefficients differ across destination types, and thin nondestination cells (Table 6: N = 5,763 Black, 2,756 Hispanic, 2,615 Asian; Table 7: 2,592 and 2,372) mean the destination-heterogeneity narrative should be read as pattern-noticing rather than evidence. The reported goodness-of-fit statistics of 1987.955 (Hispanic nondestination) and 25.422 (Asian nondestination) in Table 7 Panel B, against values below 1.4 everywhere else, indicate those specific models failed to fit — the paper cautions about the Asian cell but not the Hispanic one, and neither should inform any conclusion.
- Read the destination contrast as 'the six largest immigrant-receiving states versus everything else,' not as a test of immigrant receptivity. 'New destinations' spans 26 states plus DC and holds more sample than 'established'; 'nondestination' is 8.9% of the sample in mostly small rural states and is confounded with region, urbanicity, industry mix and cost of living. The paper's proposed mechanisms — social networks, receptivity climate, state immigration policy — are interpretation, not anything the design tests.
- Treat the unemployment results (Tables 4 and 7) as findings about short-spell unemployment among people who worked in the past year, not about labor force attachment. The sample is restricted to positive earners, which yields a 2.0% unemployment rate well below the true rate for BA holders and removes exactly the population that a mismatch story would predict is most affected. The core finding — high-linkage majors are associated with lower unemployment odds (.888 White, .868 Black, .930 Hispanic, .865 Asian) — is consistent and plausible, but it describes a favorably selected sample.
- If a specific estimate matters to your work, go to the online supplement rather than relying on the paper's summaries of it. The robustness discussion states that the 170-category reconstruction 'generally support[s] the conclusions ... although some estimates differ across specifications' without saying which — and which estimates move is precisely what determines whether a given finding survives. Tables OD1-OD7 (170 categories with broad-field fixed effects) and OB/OC (region- and division-specific linkage measures) should be inspected directly.
- When citing the foreign-born findings, note that 'foreign born' pools degree-holders educated abroad with immigrants who arrived as children and were educated in the U.S. The occupational-closure and credential-transferability mechanisms the paper invokes apply mainly to the former, and the models cannot separate them.

**Detailed Commentary:**

**Design fit.** The design is honestly matched to the question the paper actually answers, which is a descriptive one: how do linkage and match vary by race and nativity, and how do they covary with earnings and unemployment? The authors say so in the Method, in a dedicated Limitations section, and again in the Discussion, and — unusually — they reason about the direction of bias rather than just naming it. Their reasoning is sound: if marginalized students strategically select high-linkage majors while also facing wage discrimination, the linkage-earnings association is attenuated; if students accept jobs precisely because those jobs match, the match-earnings association is inflated. Readers should keep both signs in mind. Where the paper strains is in the gap between what the models estimate and what the abstract and Discussion claim. The models are OLS and logit with state and year fixed effects on cross-sectional ACS data; they support statements about adjusted associations within a state-year. The abstract's statement that racial and nativity differences 'are smaller among individuals with majors tied to specific occupations' is a statement about a conditional gap, and no conditional gap is estimated anywhere in the paper, because every outcome model in Tables 3, 4, 6 and 7 is fit separately by race. The inference runs through comparing the Linkage x Match coefficient across four separately-fitted models (.039 White, .060 Black, .069 Hispanic, .041 Asian) with different intercepts (8.610, 8.399, 8.701, 8.580) and different covariate distributions. Informally the Black-White and Hispanic-White differences are around 2.3 and 2.9 standard errors, so the underlying pattern is probably real; the Asian-White difference is essentially zero. But the paper never runs the pooled interaction model that would test this, and never computes a predicted gap at any point in the linkage-match space. The headline is therefore an interpretive extrapolation, and readers should cite the coefficient pattern, not the gap claim.

**Measurement — linkage.** The linkage index is DiPrete et al.'s mutual-information construction, simplified because ACS reports majors only for bachelor's degrees so the attainment term is unnecessary (footnote 6, defensible). It is computed on 25-to-64-year-olds whose highest credential is a bachelor's, employed full time, not self-employed, not in the armed forces, and not enrolled — sensible restrictions that track the source paper. Two features deserve more attention than they receive. First, the resulting variable is a KL divergence: bounded below at zero, unbounded above, and hence sharply right-skewed. Figure A1 makes this vivid — all 36 majors lie between roughly -0.9 and +5.0 standardized units, with the great majority packed between -1 and +1.5 and a thin tail of nuclear technologies (~+5), cosmetology/culinary arts (~+4.5), electrical/mechanical repairs (~+3.5), and library science (~+3). In an OLS with such a regressor, those few majors carry enormous leverage over every linkage coefficient in the paper, and no leverage diagnostic, winsorization, or drop-the-tail check is reported. Second, plug-in estimators of mutual information are biased upward when cell counts are small relative to the number of categories, and here the categories are roughly 470 four-digit ACS occupation codes (footnote 8). Footnote 7 sets the inclusion floor at 100 observations per major — a very low bar for estimating a distribution over that many cells — and the majors nearest that floor are exactly the small vocational fields occupying the extreme right tail. So major size and measured linkage are confounded in the direction that inflates the tail. No bias correction is mentioned. Table A1's cosmetology/culinary-arts row, which matches that major to 'Morticians, undertakers, & funeral directors,' is the kind of result small cells generate.

On standardization: Table 1 reports a sample mean of .003 and a standard deviation of 1.008 for z-linkage, which indicates the index was standardized across persons rather than across the 36 majors. This is coherent with Figure A1's shape — because the largest majors (business, social science, education) sit at the low end, person-level standardization places the mean near the bottom of the range. Readers should therefore understand a 'one standard deviation increase in linkage' as a move from roughly the median graduate to a fairly unusual major, not as a symmetric marginal change.

**Measurement — match.** Here there is a straightforward internal inconsistency worth checking before anyone builds on the paper's central interaction. The Method (p. 5) is explicit: compute ActualFreq, compute CounterfactualFreq = TotOcc x TotMaj / Tot, take the ratio, rank occupations within major by that ratio, and define the top two as matched. But Appendix Table A1's columns are headed 'Most Common Occupation' and 'Second Most Common Occupation' — frequency language — and the entries for weak-linkage majors read as frequency rankings. Ethnic studies matches to 'Secretaries & administrative assistants' and 'Human resource workers.' Liberal arts matches to 'Secretaries & administrative assistants' and 'Elementary & middle school teachers.' History matches to 'Secondary school teachers' and 'First-line supervisors of retail sales workers.' Philosophy/religion matches to 'Clergy' and 'Retail salespersons.' Under Equation 3, an occupation that is large economy-wide carries a correspondingly large counterfactual denominator, so secretaries, retail salespersons, and retail supervisors should be nearly impossible to find at the top of a ratio ranking — their ratios should hover near 1. Their appearance in four different low-linkage majors is very hard to reconcile with the stated rule. High-linkage majors are uninformative for diagnosing this, because for architecture, library science, and nursing the modal occupation and the highest-ratio occupation coincide. The consequence, if the match variable is frequency-based for at least some majors, is not neutral: it falls precisely on low-linkage majors, mislabels their 'matched' workers as secretaries and retail supervisors rather than as their fields' distinctive destinations, and thereby depresses the estimated match premium at low linkage — which mechanically steepens the Linkage x Match interaction that carries the paper's headline. This is checkable against the openICPSR deposit and should be checked.

A structural feature of the match measure also deserves flagging: exactly two occupations per major, regardless of major size or breadth. 'Matched' therefore denotes wildly different population shares across majors, and the fact that the matched share is nearly flat across race groups (14.0% to 16.2%, Table 1) is a composition artifact rather than a substantive finding. And because both linkage and match are functions of the same conditional distribution p(occupation | major), part of the Linkage x Match interaction is mechanical — footnote 9 reports a weighted correlation of .275 and Figure A2 shows linkage is visibly higher for matched workers.

**Specification.** The most consequential omission is labor supply. The covariate list is given identically in the notes to Tables 2, 3, 5 and 6 and contains no hours, no weeks worked, no full-time indicator, no occupation, and no industry. The outcome is log annual earnings on a sample defined by positive earnings. So the Match coefficients — .155 (White), .188 (Black), .170 (Hispanic), .229 (Asian) in Table 3 — combine a wage return with an employment-intensity return, and the paper offers no way to separate them. This matters most for the immigrant story: Match x Foreign Born runs .084 to .176 in Table 3 and up to .159 to .184 in Table 6's established and new destinations, and differential part-time or part-year work among unmatched immigrants would generate exactly that pattern with no wage difference at all. Note that the linkage measure itself was deliberately restricted to full-time workers; the regression sample was not.

The second specification issue is the Foreign Born coefficient. Years-in-U.S. and years-in-U.S.-squared enter the covariate list and are structurally zero for the native-born, so the Foreign Born indicator is evaluated at zero years in the country. That is a defensible parameterization but it makes the coefficient an at-arrival intercept shift, and the paper narrates it as a level gap. Table 1 puts mean years in the U.S. among the foreign-born at 20.5, and the years-in-U.S. coefficients are never reported, so the gap for the typical immigrant cannot be reconstructed from the published tables. This is why Table 7 reports White-nondestination Foreign Born odds of unemployment at 4.462 (SE 1.872) and Asian-nondestination at 4.843 (SE 5.164) — figures that would be startling as descriptions of settled immigrants but are unremarkable as descriptions of the newly arrived. The interaction terms are unaffected and remain the interpretable part of the nativity analysis.

The third issue is inference on linkage. Linkage takes 36 values. The reported standard errors come from Taylor linearization accounting for ACS strata and clustering — that is, household-level correlation — with nothing addressing the fact that the key regressor is constant within major. This is a Moulton problem with roughly 36 effective clusters, and it applies to Linkage, Linkage x Match, Linkage x Foreign Born, and the three-way term throughout Tables 3, 4, 6 and 7. Reported SEs of .001 to .014 on those terms are almost certainly too small. Marginal results should be discarded on this basis alone: the Linkage x Foreign Born term for White workers in Table 4 (1.067, p < .10) and the three-way terms in Table 3 (significant only for Hispanic at p < .05 and Asian at p < .10) are not survivable.

**Samples.** Three sample decisions shape what the results can mean. First, restriction to those whose highest credential is a bachelor's degree conditions on a post-treatment outcome. Fields that funnel graduates into professional and graduate school — biology, psychology, social science — are represented only by their non-continuing graduates, and the composition of that residual almost certainly varies by race and nativity. The paper treats this purely as a data constraint on measuring linkage (footnote 6) rather than as a selection threat to the outcome models. Second, the analytic sample is defined by positive earnings in the survey year (p. 6), which means the unemployment analyses — which the paper states use the same sample (p. 8) — measure current unemployment among people who had earnings in the prior twelve months. Hence the 2.0% unemployment rate in Table 1, below the true 2013-2017 rate for BA holders, and hence a favorably selected denominator that removes the population a mismatch story would most implicate. There is also a timing mismatch, since earnings are retrospective over twelve months while employment status is current. Third, restriction to four race categories (Table 1 shares sum exactly to 1.000: .736, .086, .090, .088) drops multiracial, Native American, and other respondents without comment.

On the data description: the Method says '1% sample of the ACS spanning the years 2013 to 2017' while the reference is to IPUMS USA Version 13.0, ACS 2013-2017 5-year sample. These are reconcilable — the 5-year file is the concatenation of five roughly 1% annual samples, and the analytic N of 1,366,603 after the restrictions is consistent with that — but anyone attempting replication needs to resolve which file and which weight variable, since 5-year and single-year ACS weights differ. Pooled multi-year ACS also nominally calls for replicate-weight variance estimation rather than Taylor linearization; the shortcut is common and the direction of error is toward understated SEs.

**The heterogeneity analysis.** Tables 5 through 7 comprise on the order of 160 focal coefficients — Table 5 has 6 columns of 7, Table 6 has 12 columns of 7, Table 7 has 12 columns of 3 — with no multiplicity adjustment and no formal test of whether any coefficient differs across destination types (the models are estimated on separate subsamples, and equality is asserted from significance-star patterns rather than tested). The destination narrative in the abstract and Discussion is built by reading this grid. Its weakest cells are also its most rhetorically active. Nondestination is only 121,371 observations overall, and within race-by-destination it collapses: Table 6 reports N = 5,763 (Black), 2,756 (Hispanic), 2,615 (Asian), and Table 7 reports 2,592 and 2,372. At a 2% unemployment rate, the Table 7 Hispanic and Asian nondestination logits are fitting roughly fifty events against state fixed effects, year fixed effects and a dozen covariates. The results look exactly like what that produces: an Asian-nondestination Linkage odds ratio of .176 (SE .114) implying an 82% reduction in unemployment odds per standard deviation, paired with a Linkage x Foreign Born odds ratio of 5.942 (SE 4.038) that reverses it. The paper's own reported diagnostics confirm the failure — the F-adjusted goodness-of-fit statistic is 1987.955 in the Hispanic nondestination column and 25.422 in the Asian nondestination column, against values between .226 and 1.335 everywhere else in Table 7. The text cautions about the Asian nondestination cell ('small sample size and the potential for spurious relationships') but not the Hispanic one, whose statistic is far worse. Table 6's Hispanic nondestination column is similarly implausible: Match at -.128 (n.s.) but Linkage x Match at .260 (SE .072) and Match x Foreign Born at .527 (SE .135), the latter a 70% earnings premium estimated off 2,756 observations. It is also worth noting that the F-adjusted goodness-of-fit statistics for the pooled match logits — 33.234 and 38.559 in Table 2, 37.387 in Table 5 — indicate substantial lack of fit and are reported without comment, though at N = 1.37 million essentially any such test rejects.

Separately, the destination taxonomy is not the immigrant-density gradient it is described as. 'New destinations' spans 26 states plus DC (footnote 4) and holds more of the sample (680,344) than the six established states (564,888), and it includes MA, MD, VA, WA, GA and NC — hardly low-immigration settings. 'Nondestination' is 8.9% of the sample across mostly small, rural, lower-cost states, confounded with region, urbanicity, industry composition and price levels. The authors also add New Jersey to Massey and Capoferro's established list and AL, NM, OK and SC to the new-destination list, and include DC where the original excludes it, with no sensitivity analysis on these choices. The mechanisms the Discussion proposes — social networks, receptivity climate, immigrant-friendly state policy — are not measured or tested anywhere.

**A textual error worth knowing about.** The introduction (p. 2) states that 'workers who are Asian, Black, Hispanic, and foreign-born are more likely to complete a college major with a stronger linkage than workers who are White and U.S. born.' Table 2 Column 1 gives the Hispanic coefficient as -.011 (SE .005, p < .05) — weaker linkage — and the Results and Discussion sections both say so correctly. Related and more subtle: the Hispanic coefficient flips sign between Table 2 Column 1 (-.011) and Column 2 (+.012), because Column 2 conditions on nativity, so U.S.-born Hispanic workers actually choose marginally higher-linkage majors and the pooled negative is driven by Hispanic immigrants (Hispanic x Foreign Born = -.028). Readers should be careful about which column any 'Hispanic effect' comes from. The text's report that 'among White individuals employed in matched occupations, a one-standard-deviation increase in linkage is associated with 3.9% higher earnings' also quotes the interaction term alone; the total for White matched workers is -.008 + .039 = 3.1%, which if anything widens the White-minority contrast the paper is drawing.

**Robustness — genuinely substantial, but summarized too thinly to lean on.** The supplement carries LPM analogues for every logit (OA1-OA4), linkage and match rebuilt at the Census-region and Census-division level (OB1-OB7, OC1-OC7), and a 170-category field-of-study reconstruction with 36 broad-field fixed effects added (OD1-OD7). The last is the most interesting design move in the paper, since it identifies linkage effects within broad field, off variation among specific sub-fields. But the text's summary is 'generally support the conclusions drawn from the primary analyses, although some estimates differ across specifications' — and which estimates differ is exactly the information a reader needs to know whether a particular finding survives. Note also that the 170-category specification does not address the two problems most likely to matter (no hours control; clustering on 36 majors), and adding 36 major fixed effects to a model whose key regressor was previously constant within major changes what the coefficient means. Footnotes 10 and 11 report a useful check: re-estimating the Table 3 and Table 6 earnings models on the reduced samples produced by perfect prediction in the unemployment logits, with substantively unchanged results.

**What to carry away.** The findings I would rely on are the sorting patterns in Table 2 — with the important caveat that the magnitudes are small (.042, -.011, .100 standardized units; R-squared .021) and only the Asian differential is noticeable — the robust positive association between working in a matched occupation and annual earnings, understood as a job-level rather than wage-rate result, and the consistent negative association between linkage and short-spell unemployment among recent earners (odds ratios .865 to .930 across all four race groups in Table 4). The findings I would treat as suggestive are the larger Linkage x Match coefficients for Black and Hispanic workers (real-looking pattern, never formally tested, and vulnerable to the Table A1 construction question and to major-level clustering) and the larger Match x Foreign Born premiums (confounded with labor supply). The findings I would not build on are anything from the nondestination columns of Tables 6 and 7, and the abstract's claim that racial and nativity disparities are smaller among matched high-linkage workers, which is not a quantity this paper estimates.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper builds a competent, well-organized sociology-of-education literature review — major choice by race/ethnicity/nativity, occupational closure, and the two DiPrete-lineage antecedents (Bol et al. 2019; Lu et al. 2024) — and its characterizations of those antecedents are broadly (though not fully verifiably) accurate. But it is bounded almost entirely within one disciplinary tradition: the economics literature on horizontal mismatch and returns to field of study is nearly absent, the immigrant-selectivity literature that supplies the leading alternative explanation for the paper's headline nativity result is missing entirely, and the paper never notes that its own estimate for Black graduates' linkage directly reverses the finding it attributes to its closest antecedent. Readers should treat the novelty claim as narrowly true about the specific measures used, not about the substantive question.

**Strengths:**

- The major-choice-by-race/ethnicity/nativity literature is covered carefully and even-handedly, including a disconfirming case (Simpson 2001, whose null result is reported rather than buried) and a plausible reconciliation via science-major attrition (Elliott et al. 1996; Astin & Astin 1992). This section is the review's best work.
- The occupational-closure framing is well sourced to the primary sociological tradition (Weber; Weeden 2002; Bol & Weeden 2015; Di Stasio & van de Werfhorst 2016; Redbird 2017; Drange & Helland 2019), and the paper correctly notes that closure operates at the skill-acquisition stage as well as the hiring stage — a genuinely useful conceptual point for readers.
- The two closest antecedents are named explicitly and the gap between them and this study is stated precisely (Bol et al. establish the linkage–outcome relationship but not by race/nativity; Lu et al. document race differences in linkage but not their consequences). Readers can locate the contribution without ambiguity.
- The paper is honest in its limitations section that estimates are descriptive, and it names the specific selection problems (into majors, occupations, and institutions) rather than gesturing at them, citing the relevant college-quality work (Dale & Krueger; Hoekstra; Long).
- Immigrant credential-transferability work is at least present (Beckhusen et al. 2013; Chiswick & Miller 2009; Tong 2010; Zeng & Xie 2004), giving readers a foothold into the skill-mismatch literature even though it is not developed.

**Weaknesses:**

- The economics literature on horizontal mismatch and field-of-study returns is essentially absent. Robst (2007, Economics of Education Review), the canonical U.S. study of major–job relatedness and earnings, is not cited at all — only the companion Robst (2008), and only for the narrow point that skills do not transfer across fields, never for its empirical earnings findings. Also missing: Nordin, Persson & Rooth (2010); Kinsler & Pavan (2015); Altonji, Blom & Meghir (2012) and Altonji, Arcidiacono & Maurel (2016); Arcidiacono (2004); the Somers et al. (2019) horizontal-mismatch meta-analysis; and Xu (2013) on STEM major–job match by race and gender. An economist reading this paper would not learn that their own literature has studied this question for two decades.
- The immigrant-selectivity literature is completely missing, and it is the leading alternative explanation for the paper's most striking result. Black immigrants show the largest match advantage in the paper (Black x Foreign Born OR = 1.89), and Asian immigrants show large linkage and match advantages — patterns that the educational-selectivity literature (Feliciano 2005; Model 2008; Hamilton 2014, 2019 on Black immigrants; Lee & Zhou 2015 on Asian hyper-selectivity) predicts on compositional grounds alone. The paper interprets these results exclusively through discrimination, networks, and closure, without acknowledging that a selectivity account exists.
- The paper never reconciles a direct contradiction with its closest antecedent. It reports that Lu et al. (2024) find 'Black graduates tend to choose fields of study with weaker linkages,' yet its own Table 2 shows Black workers choosing significantly stronger-linkage majors than White workers (+.042 SD, p < .001). The reversal is never flagged, let alone explained (plausible sources: this sample is restricted to bachelor's-as-highest-degree, excluding graduate-degree holders; different linkage construction; different covariates). Readers comparing the two papers are left to discover the conflict themselves.
- Two cited sources whose findings cut against the paper's framing are used only for background and never engaged substantively. Drange & Helland (2019) — 'The sheltering effect of occupational closure? Consequences for ethnic minorities' earnings' — asks essentially this paper's question in Norway, but is cited once in passing for the unrelated point that closure varies in degree; its actual findings are never reported. Redbird (2017) is cited as supporting closure theory, but her central result is that occupational licensure does not generate the expected wage premium and expands rather than restricts minority entry — a finding in tension with the closure mechanism the paper invokes.
- The occupational-licensing economics that most directly anticipates the paper's headline claim is absent. Blair & Chung (2019) find that occupational licensing narrows racial and gender wage gaps, precisely because formal credentials substitute for employer discretion where statistical discrimination operates — the same mechanism the paper proposes for why minorities benefit more from alignment. Kleiner & Krueger (2013) and Law & Marks (2009) are likewise missing. This omission makes the contribution look more novel than it is at the mechanism level.
- The immigrant-destination framing rests on two citations (Massey & Capoferro 2008; De Jong et al. 2017) to carry a moderator that structures roughly half the results tables. The new-destinations literature (Waters & Jimenez 2005; Singer 2004; Lichter & Johnson 2009; Flippen & Farrell-Bryan 2021) and the empirical work on state immigration enforcement and immigrant labor market outcomes (e.g., Bohn, Lofstrom & Raphael on Arizona; Amuedo-Dorantes & Bansak) are absent, so the mechanisms attributed to destination context — networks, receptivity, policy — are asserted rather than sourced.
- The Ruiz Soto (2025) citation is a Migration Policy Institute news commentary on 2025 enforcement under 'Trump 2.0,' used in the introduction to motivate the study's importance. The data are 2013–2017 ACS, so the policy environment invoked postdates the evidence by roughly eight years, and no empirical literature on enforcement effects is engaged. It functions as topical framing, not support.
- The theory section does not generate the paper's actual hypothesis. Human capital and closure theory are both marshalled to explain why minorities and immigrants are disadvantaged; the paper's central prediction — that these groups benefit MORE from alignment — is introduced instead via a paragraph of BLS descriptive statistics ('these patterns raise the possibility that...'). No testable predictions are stated, and the two frameworks are never placed in tension in a way the analysis could adjudicate.
- The major-choice literature is temporally lopsided: most of it dates from 1992-2010 (Astin & Astin 1992; Elliott et al. 1996; Leslie et al. 1998; Simpson 2001; Xie & Goyette 2003; Song & Glick 2004; Goyette & Mullen 2006; Ma 2009; Dickson 2010; Nores 2010), with almost nothing after 2014. Major composition by race has shifted substantially since — health and computing in particular — so the descriptive priors the review establishes may not describe the 2013-2017 cohort being analyzed.
- Zeng & Xie (2004) and Tong (2010) are cited for place-of-education effects, but their central implication — that immigrant earnings penalties are concentrated among the foreign-educated — is never carried into the design or the limitations, even though the ACS cannot distinguish foreign- from U.S.-educated immigrants. A citation is used for framing whose main lesson is a live threat to the paper's nativity interpretation.
- The policy recommendation — steer minority and immigrant students toward high-linkage majors — is offered without engaging any literature on whether major-steering interventions work or on their equity costs (Wiswall & Zafar on major-choice beliefs; Bleemer & Mehta on major restrictions harming underrepresented students; Baker et al. on labor-market information). The recommendation rests on a descriptive association with no supporting intervention evidence cited.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read Robst (2007, Economics of Education Review, 'Education and job match: The relatedness of college major and work') before citing this paper as first evidence on mismatch and earnings. Robst documents a substantial mismatch wage penalty in the U.S. and — critically for how this paper's 'match premium' should be read — shows the penalty depends heavily on WHY the mismatch occurred: voluntary moves for better pay or promotion carry little or no penalty, while involuntary mismatch carries a large one. Since Holzman et al. cannot observe the reason for mismatch, group differences in the match premium may partly reflect group differences in whether mismatch is voluntary, not in the returns to alignment.
- Treat the novelty claim as scoped, not general. 'The first to [link alignment to labor market outcomes] by race and nativity' is defensible only if 'alignment' means the DiPrete et al. (2017) linkage index plus the Bol et al. (2019) top-two-occupation match indicator. It is not the first study of major-job mismatch returns by race or nativity: the paper's own citation of Beckhusen et al. (2013) establishes that immigrants are less likely to hold skill-matched jobs, and the immigrant overeducation / 'brain waste' literature (Mattoo, Neagu & Ozden 2008; Chiswick & Miller 2009, 2010) addresses the substantive question directly. Cite this paper for the specific measure-by-subgroup combination; cite the predecessors for the underlying phenomenon.
- Pair the paper with the immigrant-selectivity literature before accepting its interpretation of the nativity results. Feliciano (2005) on the educational selectivity of immigrants relative to origin-country populations, Hamilton (2014, 2019) and Model (2008) on Black immigrants specifically, and Lee & Zhou (2015) on Asian hyper-selectivity all supply a compositional explanation for why foreign-born workers — especially Black and Asian immigrants — show stronger alignment and larger match premia. The paper controls for years in the U.S. and English-speaker status but nothing that proxies pre-migration selection, so this explanation is not ruled out.
- Read Blair & Chung (2019) on occupational licensing and racial/gender wage gaps alongside this paper. It reports the same directional pattern as the headline finding here — formal credentialing narrows group wage gaps — with an explicit mechanism (credentials crowd out employer discretion where statistical discrimination operates). It is the closest mechanism-level precedent and it is not cited, so the contribution is best read as extending that logic from licensure to major-occupation alignment rather than as establishing it.
- Verify the two characterizations of Lu et al. (2024) before repeating them. The paper asserts that Lu, Li & Elbers 'neither control for individual sociodemographic characteristics nor explore the intersection of race and nativity.' Decomposition designs of the kind Lu et al. use are built to partition composition from within-group differences, so 'does not control for covariates' may misdescribe a design choice rather than identify an omission. Check the original in Work, Employment and Society 38(2).
- Note the direct conflict with Lu et al. on Black graduates. This paper reports Lu et al. finding weaker linkage among Black graduates, then finds the opposite in its own Table 2. Before citing either result, check the sample definitions: Lu et al. study the 'highly educated workforce' broadly, while this paper restricts to those whose HIGHEST degree is a bachelor's — excluding graduate-degree holders, which plausibly removes a large share of high-linkage professional pathways and could differentially affect groups. The discrepancy is real and unaddressed.
- Use the ASR DOI for Bol et al. (2019), not the one printed in the reference list. The paper gives https://doi.org/10.31235/osf.io/df6as, which resolves to a SocArXiv preprint rather than the published American Sociological Review 84(2) article (10.1177/0003122419836081). Estimates and specifications can differ between preprint and published versions, and the match-measure construction this paper follows should be checked against the published text.
- Read Drange & Helland (2019) directly rather than through this paper. It is cited here only for the incidental point that closure varies in degree, but its actual subject — whether occupational closure shelters ethnic minorities' earnings — is this paper's core question in a Norwegian setting, and its findings supply the comparative evidence the review omits.
- Read Redbird (2017) for what it actually argues. This paper cites it as support for the closure framework; Redbird's finding is that licensure does not deliver the wage premium closure theory predicts and that it expands, rather than restricts, entry for women and minorities. That reading complicates the paper's theoretical story and is worth having in hand.
- For the destination-context results, supplement with the new-destinations literature the paper does not cite — Waters & Jimenez (2005) and Flippen & Farrell-Bryan (2021) for the research agenda, Singer (2004) on emerging gateways, and the empirical work on state enforcement regimes (Bohn, Lofstrom & Raphael; Amuedo-Dorantes & Bansak). The paper's destination categories are a static state-level classification carrying substantial interpretive weight; the underlying literature is more contested than the two-citation framing suggests.
- Before acting on the policy recommendation to steer students toward high-linkage majors, consult Bleemer & Mehta on the equity consequences of major access restrictions and Wiswall & Zafar on how major choice responds to information. The paper's recommendation is derived from descriptive associations, with no intervention evidence cited on either side.
- Keep in mind that Zeng & Xie (2004) and Tong (2010), which the paper cites, both identify place of education as the key moderator of immigrant earnings penalties — and the ACS cannot distinguish foreign- from U.S.-educated degree holders. The nativity results should be read as pooling two groups whose credential-recognition situations differ sharply.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Where the paper sits. This is a sociology-of-education paper that engages the sociology-of-education literature well and adjacent literatures poorly. Within its own tradition — major choice by race, ethnicity and nativity; occupational closure; the DiPrete/Bol/van de Werfhorst linkage program — the coverage is real and the positioning is legible. A reader can tell exactly what is being extended and from whom. The problem is that the question it asks has been asked, in different vocabulary, in at least three other literatures: labor economics on horizontal mismatch, immigration research on overeducation and brain waste, and the licensing literature on credentials and group wage gaps. None of these is meaningfully represented, and the effect is to make the contribution look larger than it is.

On the novelty claim specifically. The sentence 'to our knowledge, the present study is the first to do so by race and nativity' is technically defensible under a narrow reading — the specific pairing of the DiPrete et al. (2017) mutual-information linkage index with the Bol et al. (2019) top-two-occupation match indicator, estimated separately by race and by nativity with state and year fixed effects, does appear to be new. But readers will be tempted to read it more broadly, and under any broader reading it is oversold. Robst (2007) estimated mismatch penalties on U.S. earnings with demographic heterogeneity; Xu (2013) examined STEM major-job match by race and gender; Beckhusen et al. (2013), which this paper itself cites, established that highly educated immigrants are less likely to be in skill-matched work; and Mattoo, Neagu & Ozden (2008) and the Chiswick-Miller program established the immigrant credential-devaluation story. What is new here is the measurement apparatus and the subgroup stratification, not the substantive discovery that alignment returns vary by race and nativity.

The most consequential omission. The paper's headline heterogeneity result concerns immigrants, and Black and Asian immigrants in particular (Black x Foreign Born on match, OR = 1.89; Asian immigrants show both the strongest linkage advantage and the largest Linkage x Foreign Born earnings coefficients). The immigrant educational-selectivity literature predicts exactly this pattern from composition alone: immigrants are positively selected on education relative to origin populations, and Black African and Caribbean immigrants and Asian immigrants are among the most strongly selected groups entering the U.S. The paper never mentions selectivity. It interprets the results entirely through discrimination, networks, and closure. Because the ACS controls used — age, gender, years in the U.S., English-speaker status, disability, marital status, children, metro status — contain nothing that proxies pre-migration selection, the selectivity account is fully live and simply unaddressed. Any reader taking the nativity findings at face value should hold this alternative in mind.

Engagement with conflicting evidence. This is the weakest dimension. Three specific failures. First, the paper reports Lu et al. (2024) finding weaker linkage among Black graduates and then estimates the opposite sign in its own Table 2, without noticing. Second, Drange & Helland (2019) — which asks whether occupational closure shelters ethnic minorities' earnings, i.e. this paper's exact hypothesis in a Norwegian setting — appears in the bibliography but its findings are never reported; it is cited for an incidental point about closure varying in degree. Third, Redbird (2017) is enlisted as closure-theory support when her actual result runs the other way, showing that licensure fails to generate the predicted wage premium and expands minority entry. In each case the source is in the reference list, so this is not a search failure; it is a failure to engage what the sources say.

Disciplinary asymmetry. The reference list contains strong economics on the general returns to college and college quality (Bayer & Charles; Chetty et al.; Goldin; Dale & Krueger; Hoekstra; Long; Lovenheim & Smith) but almost none on the economics of field of study and job match. Altonji and coauthors, Arcidiacono, Kinsler & Pavan, Nordin et al., and Robst (2007) are all absent. The one economics-adjacent piece on fields of study, Kim, Tamborini & Sakamoto (2015), is cited once for the general observation that earnings vary by field. This matters for how readers weigh the selection discussion: the limitations section correctly identifies ability-based sorting into majors as a threat, but cites no work from the literature that has spent twenty years measuring exactly that, so the reader has no sense of how large the problem typically is.

A sorting concern the literature review would have surfaced. Table A1 makes plain that matched occupations for high-linkage majors are heavily licensed professional jobs (registered nurses, pharmacists, actuaries, civil engineers, architects) while matched occupations for low-linkage majors are secretaries, retail supervisors, and clergy. With no occupation fixed effects, the Linkage x Match interaction is partly an occupational wage-level differential rather than a return to alignment per se. The economics literature on major returns and occupational sorting is precisely where this concern is developed, and its absence means the concern is never raised in the paper.

Framing and citation hygiene. The Ruiz Soto (2025) item is an MPI news commentary on 2025 immigration enforcement used to establish the urgency of a study built on 2013-2017 data. It carries no evidentiary weight for the analysis and the paper engages no empirical work on enforcement effects on immigrant labor markets. Separately, the Bol et al. (2019) reference gives an OSF preprint DOI rather than the ASR DOI; since this paper explicitly follows Bol et al.'s guidance in constructing the match measure, readers replicating that construction should work from the published article.

Theory. Human capital and occupational closure are presented in parallel rather than in competition. Both are used to explain why minorities and immigrants are disadvantaged; neither is used to derive the paper's actual claim, that these groups benefit more from alignment. That claim enters through a paragraph of BLS labor-force statistics, hedged as 'raise the possibility.' No hypotheses are formally stated, and the empirical design cannot distinguish the two frameworks, so the theory functions as vocabulary rather than as a source of predictions.

Bottom line for readers. Cite this paper for a careful national description of how DiPrete-style linkage and Bol-style match are distributed across race and nativity groups in the 2013-2017 ACS, and for the descriptive finding that match premia are larger for Black, Hispanic, and foreign-born workers. Do not cite it as establishing that alignment causally reduces racial or nativity earnings gaps, as the first evidence that mismatch penalties vary by race or nativity, or as a complete map of what is known about field-of-study-occupation match. For that fuller picture, pair it with Robst (2007), the immigrant overeducation literature, the immigrant-selectivity literature, and Blair & Chung (2019).

Limits of this assessment. I have read the paper and its full reference list closely, but I have not re-read Bol et al. (2019), Lu et al. (2024), or Drange & Helland (2019) in the course of this review, so my claims about what those papers contain rest on prior knowledge and should be verified before being repeated — this applies particularly to the assertion that Lu et al. include no sociodemographic controls, which I flag as worth checking rather than as established. My knowledge of the horizontal-mismatch and immigrant-selectivity literatures is solid but not exhaustive, and there may be recent work (2023-2026) in either area that I am not accounting for.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

The paper is cleanly organized, plainly written, and unusually disciplined about causal language — it says "descriptive associations" in the abstract, introduction, methods, and limitations, and its Limitations section argues the likely direction of bias rather than just listing caveats. But the prose that summarizes the results is not reliable: the Introduction flatly contradicts the Results and Discussion on Hispanic linkage, the abstract and Introduction assert a linkage–earnings association that Table 3 does not show (and that the Results section itself denies), the headline "3.9%" figure for White matched workers is the interaction coefficient rather than the marginal effect, and interaction terms are repeatedly narrated as if they were total group effects.
