Readers should treat every summary sentence as a pointer to a table cell to be checked, not as a finding.

**Strengths:**

- The Method section is genuinely well taught. Linkage and match are built up in order — the mutual-information index (Eq. 1), then actual frequency, counterfactual frequency (Eq. 2), and their ratio (Eq. 3) — with a running library-science/librarian example that makes an abstract segregation measure concrete. The repeated reminder that "linkage strength is not an individual characteristic but a characteristic of society" while "Match, however, is an individual characteristic" is exactly the distinction a reader is most likely to lose, and the authors state it twice.
- Causal restraint is consistent and prominent, not buried. The Introduction closes with "All estimates should be interpreted as adjusted associations rather than causal effects"; the Method repeats it; and the Limitations section stands as its own heading between Results and Discussion (p. 11), where it is easy to find rather than tucked into the last paragraphs of the Discussion. That section also does real work — it argues that self-selection into high-linkage majors by marginalized groups would bias the linkage–earnings association "toward zero," and that selective sorting into matched jobs would "bias the match–earnings relationship upward," i.e., it names the direction in each case.
- Table notes are complete and self-contained. Every regression table states the estimator, that survey weights are applied, that year and state fixed effects are included, the full covariate list, and — in Table 2 — the reference categories ("The reference group for race is White, while the reference group for foreign-born is native-born"). Logit tables say explicitly that coefficients are odds ratios. A reader who reads only a table knows what they are looking at.
- Robustness work is signposted rather than hidden. Footnote 5 (region/division-specific linkage measures), footnote 7 (majors with <100 observations dropped, N = 68 military technologies), footnotes 10 and 11 (perfect-prediction state drops, with the earnings models re-estimated on the reduced samples), and the four online LPM replications (OA1–OA4) plus the 170-category field-of-study check (OD1–OD7) are all named at the point where the relevant result appears.
- The theoretical frame is not ornamental. Human capital theory and occupational closure theory are set up in the Background as making distinguishable predictions, and the Discussion returns to both and assigns findings to each — the choice of high-linkage majors combined with low match rates is read through closure, the match earnings premium through human capital.

**Weaknesses:**

- FLAT CONTRADICTION ON HISPANIC LINKAGE. Introduction, p. 2: "Our results show that workers who are Asian, Black, Hispanic, and foreign-born are more likely to complete a college major with a stronger linkage than workers who are White and U.S. born." Results, p. 8: "Hispanic workers tend to choose majors with weaker linkage." Discussion, p. 14: "Black and Asian workers are more likely to choose majors with strong linkages, while Hispanic workers are less likely to do so." Table 2, Column 1, Hispanic = −.011* (SE .005). The Introduction is wrong on the sign; the Results and Discussion agree with the table. A reader who reads only the Introduction takes away the opposite of the paper's own finding.
- THE ABSTRACT AND INTRODUCTION OVERSTATE THE LINKAGE–EARNINGS RESULT. Abstract: "we find that earning bachelor's degrees in majors with strong linkage is associated with higher earnings—particularly for workers in matched occupations." Introduction, p. 2: "linkage is positively associated with earnings—particularly among individuals in matched occupations." Table 3 Linkage main effects: White −.008*** (.001), Black .000 (.005), Hispanic −.001 (.005), Asian .012 (.009). Not one group shows a positive, significant linkage–earnings association; the only significant estimate is negative. The Results section says so plainly — "we find little evidence that linkage alone is associated with earnings … with the exception of White workers, for whom we observe a small negative association" — which means the abstract's "particularly" should be "only," and the abstract contradicts the paper's own results text. The unemployment half of that abstract sentence does hold (Table 4 Linkage ORs .888***, .868***, .930*, .865*, all < 1).
- THE 3.9% FIGURE IS THE WRONG QUANTITY. Results, p. 9: "among White individuals employed in matched occupations, a one-standard-deviation increase in linkage is associated with 3.9% higher earnings." For a matched White worker the marginal effect is Linkage + Linkage × Match = −.008 + .039 = .031, i.e. ~3.1%, not 3.9%. The text has quoted the Linkage × Match coefficient (.039***) alone — one sentence after explicitly acknowledging that the interaction is "offsetting the negative baseline association discussed earlier." The comparison figures are similarly the raw interaction coefficients (Black .060***, Hispanic .069***); for Black the main effect is .000 so 6.0% happens to be right, and for Hispanic the true marginal effect is .068 rather than the quoted 6.9%. The direction of the paper's claim survives — the gap is actually wider (3.1 vs. 6.0/6.8) — but the specific White number should not be quoted.
- "HIGHER AMONG RACIAL AND ETHNIC MINORITIES" IS TOO BROAD. Results, p. 9: "Notably, these premiums are higher among racial and ethnic minorities than among White workers." Table 3 Linkage × Match: White .039***, Black .060***, Hispanic .069***, Asian .041**. Asian (.041) is statistically and substantively indistinguishable from White (.039). The claim holds for Black and Hispanic only, which is what the very next sentence and the abstract actually name — the generalizing sentence is the one that misfires.
- INTERACTION COEFFICIENTS ARE NARRATED AS TOTAL EFFECTS, INCONSISTENTLY. Results on Table 2, p. 8: "Among Hispanic workers, immigrants tend to select majors with weaker linkage … than their native-born Hispanic counterparts." Table 2 Column 2: Foreign Born = .207***, Hispanic × Foreign Born = −.028**. Hispanic immigrants versus Hispanic natives is .207 − .028 = +.179 — Hispanic immigrants choose *stronger*-linkage majors than Hispanic natives; the interaction only says their immigrant premium is smaller than White immigrants'. The paper knows how to do this correctly — three pages later, discussing Table 5, it writes "the positive coefficients for Foreign-Born indicate that immigrants of all racial and ethnic backgrounds remain more likely than native-born individuals to select strong-linkage majors." The same slippage recurs on Table 5's match columns: "Black immigrants … are more likely to work in a matched occupation in established and new destinations" rests on Black × Foreign Born = 1.892*** / 1.849***, but combined with Foreign Born = .535*** / .517*** the odds for Black immigrants are roughly at parity with Black natives, and "Asian immigrants … are more likely to work in a matched occupation across all destination contexts" (Asian × FB = 1.298***, 1.131*, 1.593*) becomes .535 × 1.298 = .69 against Asian natives.
- THE FOREIGN-BORN COEFFICIENTS ARE NOT ANCHORED. Results, p. 9: "Foreign-born individuals face a disadvantage, with their earnings substantially lower than those of native-born individuals across all racial and ethnic groups." Table 3 Foreign Born: −.292***, −.607***, −.642***, −.356*** — roughly 25% to 47% lower earnings. But the covariate list (Table 2 note, Eq. 4/5) includes "years in the United States, years in the United States squared," which are zero for natives, and the model includes Linkage × FB, Match × FB, and the triple interaction. The coefficient therefore describes an unmatched immigrant, at mean linkage, with zero years in the United States — not the average immigrant BA holder. No sentence or note anywhere states the evaluation point, and no marginal effects or predicted values are reported. A reader who quotes "−.642 means Hispanic immigrants earn 47% less" would be quoting something the paper never estimated.
- TABLE A1'S HEADERS NAME THE WRONG CONSTRUCT. The Method (p. 6) defines matched occupations as the top two by the actual-to-counterfactual *ratio*: "Finally, we rank occupations by their ratio values within each college major … we define the two occupations with the highest ratio values as matched occupations (see Table A1)." Table A1's columns are headed "Most Common Occupation" and "Second Most Common Occupation," which is the actual-frequency ranking the Method explicitly rejects, and the table carries no note at all. The entries make the confusion visible — liberal arts and ethnic studies both map to "Secretaries & administrative assistants," cosmetology/culinary arts to "Morticians, undertakers, & funeral directors" — and a reader taking the headers literally will draw the wrong conclusion about what "match" means throughout the paper.

  *See the correction note in the Methods sub-review above.*

- THE UNEMPLOYMENT OUTCOME IS NEVER RECONCILED WITH THE SAMPLE. The analytic sample "comprises 1,366,603 individuals reporting positive earnings in the survey year" (p. 7), and the Method states "For consistency, the unemployment analyses use the same analytic sample as the earnings analyses" (p. 8). Unemployment is never defined, and the paper never explains how a sample restricted to positive earners contains the 2.0% unemployed in Table 1 (presumably measured at the survey reference week after positive earnings in the prior twelve months). Nothing in the text alerts the reader that Tables 4 and 7 estimate unemployment conditional on having worked, which is a nonstandard and consequential restriction.
- "F-ADJUSTED GOODNESS-OF-FIT" IS UNEXPLAINED AND UNUSABLE. The row appears in Tables 2, 4, 5, and 7 with no definition, no p-value, no direction, and no note. The values span four orders of magnitude — .226 (Table 7, Black established) to 1987.955 (Table 7 Panel B, Column 3, Hispanic nondestination) and 25.422 (Panel B, Column 6, Asian nondestination), against 33.234 / 38.559 in Table 2 and .371–.735 in Table 4. A reader cannot tell whether high is good or bad, and therefore cannot tell that two of the destination-split models are apparently badly misfit.
- SELECTIVE CAUTION IN THE SMALL CELLS. The text does flag one fragile estimate — "While a similar pattern is observed for Asian workers in nondestination states, this finding should be interpreted with caution due to the small sample size and the potential for spurious relationships" (Table 7 Panel B, Column 6: Linkage OR .176** with SE .114, Linkage × FB 5.942** with SE 4.038, N = 2,372). But the equally fragile Hispanic nondestination models get no such warning, and are instead leaned on: Table 6 Panel B, Column 3 (N = 2,756) has a *negative and insignificant* Match main effect (−.128, SE .104) alongside Match × Foreign Born = .527*** and Linkage × Match = .260***, and the text folds it into "Similar patterns are observed for … Hispanic immigrants across all destination contexts" without noting that the base match premium is absent there. The corresponding Table 7 cell carries the 1987.955 fit statistic. Likewise "foreign-born workers of all races face a disadvantage in established immigrant destinations, new immigrant destinations, and nondestinations" is hedged only by "in general" — Table 6 Panel B, Column 6 has Asian nondestination Foreign Born = −.112, n.s. (SE .098), and Table 6 Panel B, Column 6 Match = .242, n.s. (SE .169) is never acknowledged.
- TABLE 6/7 PANEL REFERENCES ARE AMBIGUOUS. Results, p. 11: "Asian immigrants in established immigrant destinations … as indicated by the positive and statistically significant coefficient for Match × Foreign Born (.124)" cites "(see Column 4)." The .124*** value is correct — but it is in Table 6 **Panel B**, Column 4. Panel A also has a Column 4 (Black, established), whose Match × Foreign Born is .159***. Both panels reuse the labels (1)–(6), and the text never names the panel.
- FIGURE A1 IS BURIED AND ITS AXIS HIDES THE KEY FACT. The figure is the only place a reader can see what the linkage measure means, yet it sits on p. 19 and is referenced once. It shows the distribution is severely right-skewed: about twenty of the thirty-six majors sit in a narrow band between roughly −0.6 and 0 SD, with a long tail up to nuclear technologies at ~+4.5 SD, and the x-axis is drawn from −5.0 to +5.0, leaving the entire left half empty. Figure A2 confirms it (Match = 0 median ≈ −0.4, Match = 1 median ≈ +0.9). Nothing in the text tells the reader that the "one-standard-deviation increase in linkage" underlying every headline number is not a move most graduates could make — the SD is set by a handful of small tail majors, and the two match groups are being compared over quite different linkage supports.
- MINOR DATA-DESCRIPTION FRICTION. The Method says "we use individual-level data from the 1% sample of the ACS spanning the years 2013 to 2017 (Ruggles et al., 2023)," while the reference is to "[American Community Survey 2013–2017 5-year sample dataset]." The two are reconcilable (the 5-year file pools annual 1% samples), and the N of 1,366,603 is consistent with the 5-year file, but a reader checking the sampling design against the Taylor-linearized standard errors has to work that out unaided.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read Table 3 (p. 9) before you read the abstract's claims, and treat it as the paper's load-bearing exhibit. Everything the article is cited for lives in seven rows across four columns.
- For any statement about linkage and earnings, add the Linkage main effect to the Linkage × Match coefficient before quoting a number. For matched workers the effects are White .031, Black .060, Hispanic .068, Asian .053 — not the 3.9%/6.0%/6.9% the text gives. Do not quote 3.9% for White matched workers.
- Treat the Introduction's third paragraph (p. 2) as unreliable on Hispanic linkage; the Results (p. 8) and Discussion (p. 14) agree with Table 2, Column 1 (−.011*) and the Introduction does not. If you need to cite the paper on Hispanic major choice, cite the table cell, not the summary sentence.
- Whenever the text says a group of immigrants is 'more' or 'less' likely to do something, check whether the sentence is describing an interaction coefficient or a total effect, and against which reference group. Multiply the Foreign Born main effect through before drawing a conclusion — this is where the paper's prose is loosest, most notably on Table 2 Column 2 (Hispanic immigrants) and Table 5 Columns 4–6 (Black and Asian immigrants).
- Do not read the Foreign Born coefficients in Tables 3, 4, 6, and 7 as the average immigrant penalty. Years in the United States and its square are in the model and are zero for natives, so the coefficient describes an immigrant with zero years in the country, unmatched, at mean linkage.
- Read Table A1 with the Method's definition in hand (p. 6, the ratio ranking), not with its own column headers. The headers say 'most common'; the construct is the highest actual-to-counterfactual ratio, which is why liberal arts maps to secretaries and cosmetology/culinary arts to morticians.
- Look at Figures A1 and A2 (pp. 19–20) early, not as an afterthought. They are the only place the linkage scale is made visible, and they show it is heavily right-skewed with almost nothing below −1 SD — essential context for interpreting any 'one-standard-deviation increase.'
- Tables 5–7 can be skimmed if you want the paper's core finding; they are thirty subgroup models with no multiple-comparison adjustment, several fit on cells of 2,372–5,763 observations. If you do use them, restrict yourself to the established- and new-destination columns and treat every nondestination cell as exploratory — including the Hispanic nondestination models (Table 6 Panel B Col. 3 and Table 7 Panel B Col. 3, F-adjusted goodness-of-fit 1987.955), which the text does not flag even though it flags the comparably fragile Asian cell.
- Ignore the 'F-adjusted goodness-of-fit' rows unless you can independently identify the test; the paper gives no definition, direction, or p-value, and the values range from .226 to 1987.955.
- Note that Tables 6 and 7 each contain two panels that both number their columns (1)–(6). The text's '(see Column 4)' on p. 11 refers to Panel B; check the panel before matching a cited number to a cell.
- Before citing the paper on unemployment, note that the unemployment models are estimated on the same sample of individuals 'reporting positive earnings in the survey year.' The paper never explains this, and it means Tables 4 and 7 describe unemployment conditional on having had earnings.
- The Limitations section (pp. 11–13) is worth reading in full and is honestly placed — it is the one part of the paper where the prose is, if anything, more cautious than the tables require. The Background section can be skimmed by anyone already familiar with human capital and occupational closure theory.

**Detailed Commentary:**

VERIFICATION NOTE: Every discrepancy asserted above was checked against a layout-preserving extraction of the published PDF (Tables 3, 6, and 7 re-extracted with column alignment intact; Figures A1 and A2 rendered and inspected). Where a plausible-looking problem did not survive checking, I have not asserted it — in particular, the significance-star legends are internally consistent with usage: Table 2's legend omits '+' and the table contains no '+' values; Table 4's legend omits '**' and the table contains no '**' values (Black Linkage = .868*** and Black Linkage × Foreign Born = .868* are distinct cells). The legends differ across tables, but each matches its own contents. Table 1's reported figures also check out exactly: \$75,026 (75,025.570), \$71,046 (71,045.870), the 14.0%–16.2% match range (.140–.162), and the foreign-born shares 76.9/39.5/17.9/5.8.

WHERE THE PROSE AND THE TABLES PART COMPANY. The paper's failures are concentrated in the summarizing sentences — abstract, Introduction, and the topic sentences of results paragraphs — while the sentence-by-sentence walk-throughs of individual tables are largely accurate. The Table 5 narrative, for instance, is verifiable nearly line by line: 'Black, Hispanic, and Asian individuals are more likely to choose college majors with strong linkages … in established immigrant destination states' matches Column 1 (.060***, .027***, .052***); 'we find no significant differences among racial and ethnic groups in new destination and nondestination states' matches Columns 2 and 3 (.003, .009, −.005; −.016, −.033, .008, none significant); 'Black workers are less likely than White workers to work in a matched occupation, regardless of state context' matches Columns 4–6 (.848***, .777***, .759***); and 'Hispanic and Asian workers are more likely to work in a matched occupation in established destination states but are less likely to do so in nondestination states' matches Hispanic 1.084*** / .796* and Asian 1.117*** / .574** (the insignificant middle column, .980 and .950, is passed over silently but the 'but' construction does not misrepresent it). Likewise the Table 6 claim 'Similar patterns are observed for White immigrants in established destinations, Black immigrants in established and new destinations, and Hispanic immigrants across all destination contexts' checks out cell by cell on Match × Foreign Born: White established .118***, Black established .159***, Black new .168***, Hispanic established .159***, Hispanic new .184***, Hispanic nondestination .527***. And 'there is more limited evidence that strong-linkage majors provide an earnings premium for foreign-born workers, except for Asian immigrants' is exactly right — Linkage × Foreign Born is significant in all three Asian columns (.075***, .114***, .142*) and in none of the White, Black, or Hispanic columns (White new .019+ is the only near miss).

That accuracy in the detail makes the failures in the summaries more, not less, consequential: a reader who skims will be misled precisely where they are least likely to check. The Introduction's assertion that Hispanic workers choose stronger-linkage majors is contradicted by Table 2 Column 1 (−.011*) and by the paper's own Results and Discussion. The abstract's 'earning bachelor's degrees in majors with strong linkage is associated with higher earnings' is contradicted by all four Linkage main effects in Table 3 (−.008***, .000, −.001, .012) and by the Results paragraph that opens 'we find little evidence that linkage alone is associated with earnings.' The 3.9% figure quotes an interaction coefficient as a marginal effect two sentences after the text has explained why that is wrong. These are the sentences that will be quoted in other papers.

WHAT THE ABSTRACT GETS RIGHT. The abstract's 'lower unemployment' is supported (Table 4 Linkage ORs .888***, .868***, .930*, .865*, all below 1 and significant). Its 'Black, Hispanic, and foreign-born workers appear to benefit more from major–occupation alignment than White and U.S.-born workers' does not misstate the Asian result — it simply omits Asian workers, whose Linkage × Match (.041**) is indistinguishable from White (.039***). That omission is a fair reading of the table, though a reader who mentally substitutes 'racial minorities' for the enumerated list will be wrong, and the Results section makes exactly that substitution. The abstract's closing sentence — 'the study findings provide descriptive evidence' — is a genuine and welcome piece of restraint at the point of maximum readership. Worth noting too that Asian workers show the *largest* raw match premium of any group (Match = .229***, versus White .155***), a fact neither the abstract nor the Discussion mentions.

NAVIGATION. The load-bearing evidence is Table 3, and secondarily Table 2 (who chooses what) and Table 4 (unemployment). Tables 5–7 are twelve pages of subgroup splits producing thirty models, several on samples between 2,372 and 5,763, with no correction for multiple comparisons and no discussion of statistical power; they generate the Discussion's regional policy recommendations, which is a heavier load than those cells can bear. A time-constrained reader can stop after Table 4 and the Limitations section and lose nothing they could safely cite. The Background can be skimmed; the Method should not be, because the meaning of both key variables is established there and nowhere else, and because the Table A1 mislabeling means the appendix alone will actively mislead about what 'match' is. The Limitations section is honestly placed and honestly worded, and is the one place where the prose is more conservative than the tables require.

EXHIBITS AS EXHIBITS. The regression tables are complete and well-noted; the figures are not. Figure A1 is the paper's single most informative exhibit about what the linkage measure actually is, and it is on p. 19 with one in-text mention. Its axis runs −5.0 to +5.0 while all thirty-six majors fall between roughly −0.6 and +4.5, so half the plot is blank and the dense cluster of twenty low-linkage majors is compressed into an unreadable band. Figure A2 is reproduced small enough that its axis labels are near-illegible and carries no note, no medians, and no N. Together they establish that the linkage variable is bounded near −1 SD below and has a long thin right tail — which is what makes 'a one-standard-deviation increase in linkage' a counterfactual most graduates cannot enact, and which the text never says. Table A1's headers, finally, describe a different quantity from the one the Method defines, and the table has no note to catch the error.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper's genuine contribution is filling a specific empirical gap: it is, as far as I can tell, the first U.S. study to connect DiPrete et al.'s (2017) major–occupation linkage measure and Bol et al.'s (2019) match indicator to earnings and unemployment separately by race and nativity, and then to stratify those associations by immigrant-destination state context. The execution is competent and transparent at scale (N = 1,366,603; openICPSR deposit; several appendix robustness sets), and the descriptive facts it establishes about who chooses high-linkage majors and who ends up matched are worth having on the record. But the paper's most quotable claims — that minorities and immigrants "benefit more" from alignment and that disparities are "smaller" among aligned workers — run ahead of what the tables actually demonstrate, and the policy recommendations run further ahead still.

**Strengths:**

- Fills a clearly identified and real gap. Lu et al. (2024) documented racial differences in linkage but stopped short of outcomes; Bol et al. (2019) estimated outcome associations for the U.S. but pooled across race, nativity, and region. Connecting the two is an obvious next step that nobody had taken, and the paper takes it cleanly.
- The immigrant-destination stratification (established / new / nondestination, following Massey & Capoferro 2008) is the most original analytic move in the paper. It reveals that the pooled race coefficients hide substantial geographic heterogeneity — Hispanic and Asian workers are MORE likely to be matched than White workers in established destinations (ORs 1.084, 1.117) but LESS likely in nondestinations (.796, .574) — a fact the pooled Table 2 estimates (.932, 1.151) would never surface.
- The single most robust and most useful finding is the occupational match premium: .155–.229 log points, significant at p < .001 in every racial group and in essentially every destination cell, and larger for foreign-born workers in every group (Match × Foreign Born .078–.176). This is a well-powered, stable, replicable fact and the paper's strongest citable output.
- Honest about design limits in the right places. The Limitations section names selection into majors, occupations, and institutions; signs the likely direction of bias in each case; concedes the match–earnings relationship is probably biased upward; and states plainly that all estimates are adjusted associations. The nontrivial robustness program (170-category linkage with 36-field-of-study fixed effects, Census-region and -division linkage measures, LPM analogues, refitting earnings models on the reduced unemployment samples) reflects real diligence.
- Public data, public code, a documented measure-construction procedure, and a full matched-occupation crosswalk (Table A1) make this straightforward for others to build on or contest — which matters more than usual for a paper whose central variables are constructed rather than observed.

**Weaknesses:**

- The headline claim that racial and nativity disparities are "smaller among individuals with majors tied to specific occupations" is never actually estimated. Every outcome model is run on a separate racial subsample (Tables 3, 4, 6, 7). Subsample regressions with their own intercepts and their own covariate slopes cannot tell you what the White–Black earnings gap is at match = 1 versus match = 0. There is no pooled model with race × alignment interactions and no formal test that any cross-group difference is statistically distinguishable. The paper's most quotable sentence is an inference from side-by-side coefficients, not a result.
- The 'benefit more from linkage' narrative rests on a 2–3 log-point difference in one interaction term. Linkage × Match is .039 (White), .060 (Black), .069 (Hispanic), .041 (Asian). By eyeball the Black–White and Hispanic–White contrasts would likely survive a formal test; the Asian–White contrast (.041 vs .039) is nil, yet the Discussion generalizes to 'racial and ethnic minorities.' More important, this differential applies only to the 15.7% of workers who are matched, on top of a linkage main effect that is zero or slightly negative — so the substantive scope of the 'minorities benefit more' claim is much narrower than the abstract conveys.
- The Foreign Born main effects (−.292 to −.642) are estimated alongside years-in-U.S. and years-in-U.S.-squared, so they identify the immigrant–native gap at zero years in the country, not the average immigrant penalty. Readers who quote '-.64 for Hispanic immigrants' as the immigrant earnings disadvantage will be badly wrong, and the paper's framing that the match premium 'partially offsets' this disadvantage is arithmetic against an arrival-year intercept rather than against a typical immigrant. This parameterization is never discussed.
- Restricting to bachelor's-only holders is not a neutral sample restriction — it deforms the linkage measure itself. The tight major-to-occupation pathways for biology, psychology, philosophy, and pre-law run through graduate school, so stripping graduate-degree holders out makes those fields look diffuse and low-linkage by construction. Table A1 shows what 'match' then means: Law → paralegals; Philosophy/religion → clergy and retail salespersons; History → secondary teachers and first-line retail supervisors; Ethnic studies and Liberal arts → secretaries and administrative assistants. 'Matched' therefore denotes something quite different (and differently paid) across majors, and because groups are unevenly distributed across majors, the racial heterogeneity in the match premium is partly compositional. The restriction also selects on not obtaining an advanced degree, which is itself patterned by race and nativity.
- The policy recommendations — steer minorities toward high-linkage majors, extend 60×30TX with targeted supports, target immigrant-destination states — do not follow from the estimates. Linkage on its own carries no earnings return (and a negative one for White workers); the return exists only conditional on match, and the paper's own Table 2 shows Black, Hispanic, and foreign-born workers are the least likely to achieve match. A policy pushing these groups into high-linkage majors without changing their matching probability could plausibly leave them worse off, precisely the tradeoff (Robst 2008) the Background raises and the Discussion drops. There is also no acknowledgment that alignment premiums are equilibrium quantities that would not survive a large-scale supply shift.
- The regional-targeting recommendation leans on the thinnest cells in the paper. Nondestination subsamples are 5,763 (Black), 2,756 (Hispanic), and 2,615 (Asian), and they produce visibly unstable estimates: Linkage × Match = .260 for Hispanics in nondestinations, an unemployment odds ratio of .176 with Linkage × Foreign Born = 5.942 for Asians there. The paper flags the Asian case but the general fragility of the destination contrast — which is the basis for a policy claim — is understated.
- The 60×30TX framing is a hook rather than an analysis. Texas is pooled into 'established destinations' with five other states and never examined separately; nothing in the paper speaks to Texas specifically, or to any state plan's actual levers.
- Cross-sectional 2013–2017 data pooled over ages 25–64 measure linkage from contemporaneous occupational flows and apply it to degrees earned up to forty years earlier, mixing cohorts and career stages in a way that goes unaddressed.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- CITE IT FOR: the occupational match earnings premium among U.S. bachelor's-only workers (roughly .16–.23 log points), and for the finding that this premium is consistently larger for foreign-born than U.S.-born workers within every racial group. This is the paper's best-powered, most stable result and holds across LPM, alternative-linkage, and regional-measure specifications.
- CITE IT FOR: the descriptive alignment profile by race and nativity — immigrants of all racial groups choose higher-linkage majors than the U.S.-born yet are markedly less likely to work in matched occupations (OR ≈ .50–.55); Black workers choose higher-linkage majors but match less often; Asian workers do better on both. This is the paper's clearest advance over Lu et al. (2024) and is well supported.
- CITE IT FOR: the demonstration that pooled national estimates conceal destination-context heterogeneity — the sign of the Hispanic and Asian match differential flips between established-destination and nondestination states. Cite the existence of the heterogeneity, not the magnitudes in nondestination cells.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: the claim that major–occupation alignment narrows racial or nativity earnings gaps. No model in the paper estimates a between-group gap or interacts race with alignment in a pooled specification, so no disparity is ever tested, let alone shown to shrink.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: the claim that minorities 'benefit more' from linkage as a general proposition. The differential is a 2–3 log-point gap in an interaction term, untested across groups, applying only to the 15.7% of workers who are matched, and it is absent for Asian workers.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: any magnitude of the immigrant earnings penalty. The Foreign Born coefficients are conditioned on a years-in-U.S. quadratic and describe newly arrived immigrants, not immigrants on average.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: policy claims that steering students into high-linkage majors will raise earnings or reduce gaps. Linkage alone shows no earnings association; the premium requires matching, which the paper shows is the step where minority and immigrant workers fall behind, and no analysis here identifies a lever that changes matching.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: cross-major comparisons of linkage strength as a general characterization of fields. The bachelor's-only restriction removes graduate-gated career pathways and mechanically depresses linkage for fields whose tight destinations require an advanced degree.
- STILL OPEN: whether any of this is causal. Selection into majors, occupations, and institutions is unaddressed by design, and the authors state the match–earnings association is likely biased upward. Longitudinal or quasi-experimental work — NLSY, state administrative data, institution-level records — is needed before any returns interpretation.
- STILL OPEN: how much of the racial earnings gap among bachelor's holders alignment could account for. A decomposition, which this paper's framing implies but never performs, remains the obvious next study.
- STILL OPEN: mechanisms. Why immigrants who select high-linkage majors so consistently fail to reach matched occupations — credential recognition, licensure barriers, legal status, network access, discrimination — is the substantively important question this paper raises and leaves entirely to future work.
- STILL OPEN: whether the destination-context differences reflect networks, state policy, labor demand composition, or selective migration. The paper offers all of these as interpretations and can adjudicate among none.

**Detailed Commentary:**

WHAT IS ACTUALLY NEW. Strip away the framing and the increment is well-defined: Bol et al. (2019) showed that linkage and match predict earnings and unemployment, including in the U.S., pooling across groups; Lu et al. (2024) showed that linkage of chosen majors differs by race, without connecting it to outcomes. Holzman et al. cross those two — outcome associations, estimated separately by race and by nativity, with sociodemographic controls and state/year fixed effects — and add a third cut nobody had tried, the immigrant-destination state typology. The claim to be first on the race-and-nativity-by-outcome cell appears defensible. Everything else in the paper is confirmatory: that minorities and immigrants pick more vocationally specific majors (Ma 2009; Dickson 2010; Goyette & Mullen 2006; Nores 2010), that immigrants are disproportionately mismatched (Beckhusen et al. 2013), and that match pays (Bol et al. 2019). The paper is candid about most of this, though it oversells its fixed-effects design as an advance 'prior studies have not addressed' — state and year fixed effects on pooled cross-sections of 25-to-64-year-olds absorb very little of the selection problem that actually threatens these estimates.

THE GAP BETWEEN THE QUOTABLE AND THE SUPPORTED. This is the central issue a reader needs to understand. The abstract makes two claims that will get cited: minorities and immigrants 'benefit more' from alignment, and disparities are 'smaller' among aligned workers. The second is not tested anywhere in the paper. Every outcome model in Tables 3, 4, 6, and 7 is fit on a separate racial subsample, so each group has its own intercept and its own slope on every covariate. Nothing in that design produces an estimate of a between-group gap, at any value of match or linkage. To support 'disparities are smaller among aligned workers' you would need a pooled model with race × match and race × linkage × match terms and a test of the interaction; there is none. The claim is a reading of side-by-side coefficients, and readers should treat it as a hypothesis the paper motivates rather than a finding it establishes.

The first claim is testable from the reported numbers but is also never formally tested. Linkage × Match runs .039 (SE .002) for White, .060 (.009) for Black, .069 (.010) for Hispanic, .041 (.014) for Asian. Approximate contrasts against White give t ≈ 2.3 for Black and t ≈ 2.9 for Hispanic — likely significant, but the reader has to do this arithmetic themselves, and the Asian contrast is essentially zero. That last point matters because the Discussion generalizes to 'racial and ethnic minorities' when the pattern is really Black and Hispanic only. And the substantive scope is narrow in a way the abstract obscures: linkage has no earnings association on its own (it is a precisely estimated −.008 for White workers and statistically zero for the other three groups), so the entire differential lives inside the 15.7% of the sample who are matched — a group that, by the paper's own Table 2, Black, Hispanic, and foreign-born workers are less likely to belong to. A cleaner one-line summary of Table 3 than the abstract's would be: match pays a lot, everywhere; linkage pays nothing unless you match; and among matched workers the linkage slope is a couple of points steeper for Black and Hispanic workers.

THE FOREIGN BORN COEFFICIENTS. The Foreign Born main effects run −.292 (White) to −.642 (Hispanic), which as raw immigrant earnings penalties for bachelor's holders would be implausibly large. They are not raw penalties: the models include years in the U.S. and its square, so the dummy is evaluated at zero years — the gap at arrival. Immigrant earnings profiles converge with duration, and the average immigrant in this sample has been in the country roughly 20 years (Table 1). The paper never notes this, and the interpretive consequence is real: the recurring 'match partially offsets the immigrant disadvantage' framing (Match × Foreign Born of .078–.176 set against a main effect of −.29 to −.64) compares a premium for the average matched immigrant against an intercept for a hypothetical just-arrived one. The Match × Foreign Born result itself is solid and citable; the offsetting arithmetic built around it is not.

WHAT THE MEASURE CAN AND CANNOT BEAR. Two construction choices constrain how far the results travel. First, the bachelor's-only restriction. This is presented as a sample definition but it reshapes the linkage measure, because the majors with the tightest real-world occupational destinations — biology to medicine, psychology to clinical practice, political science and philosophy to law — reach those destinations through graduate school, and stripping graduate-degree holders out makes those fields look occupationally diffuse by construction. Table A1 is the tell: Law matches to paralegals; Philosophy/religion to clergy and retail salespersons; History to secondary teachers and first-line retail supervisors; Ethnic studies and Liberal arts both to secretaries and administrative assistants. So 'matched' means 'radiation therapist' for one major and 'administrative assistant' for another, and the pooled match premium averages over those. Because racial and nativity groups are distributed differently across majors, the group differences in the match premium are partly differences in what matching means for each group's modal major — a compositional channel the paper does not examine. The restriction also conditions on not having earned an advanced degree, which is itself patterned by race and nativity (77% of the Asian sample is foreign-born, and Asian bachelor's holders have unusually high graduate attainment, so the Asian cell here is a selected residual).

Second, match is a binary flag for the top two occupations by actual-to-counterfactual ratio, capturing 15.7% of workers. The other 84% include people in the third-through-tenth most related occupations alongside people doing something entirely unrelated. A coarser instrument than the substantive question really wants, and it means the match premium is an average over a heterogeneous treated category compared against a heterogeneous control.

DESTINATION CONTEXT: THE BEST IDEA, THE THINNEST EVIDENCE. The destination stratification is the paper's most interesting original move, and Table 5 delivers a genuinely informative result: the pooled race coefficients in Table 2 mask sign reversals across state types. That is worth citing on its own. But the destination analysis is also where the sample runs out. Nondestination cells hold 5,763 Black, 2,756 Hispanic, and 2,615 Asian workers, and they generate exactly the estimates you would expect from cells that size — Linkage × Match of .260 for Hispanics in nondestinations, an unemployment odds ratio of .176 paired with a Linkage × Foreign Born of 5.942 for Asians there. The paper cautions on the Asian case specifically but then builds a policy recommendation (target established and new destinations, since alignment matters less in nondestinations) on the established-versus-nondestination contrast, which is precisely the comparison the thin cells cannot support. A 'no detectable effect in nondestinations' reading here is far more likely to be a power statement than a substantive one.

POLICY REACH. The Discussion recommends guiding minorities toward high-linkage majors, extending 60×30TX with targeted support for underserved groups, and prioritizing immigrant-destination states. Each outruns the evidence in a distinct way. The first is contradicted by the paper's own estimates: linkage carries no earnings return unless paired with match, and the groups being targeted are the ones least likely to match; the Background even cites Robst (2008) on the narrowing of transferable options that specific majors impose, then never returns to it. The second attaches to a state plan the paper never analyzes — Texas is folded into 'established destinations' with five other states and never separated. The third rests on the thinnest cells. Underneath all three sits an equilibrium problem no descriptive design can touch: alignment premiums are prices, and a policy that substantially shifts major composition changes them. This is not a fatal flaw — descriptive papers routinely gesture at policy — but the gesturing here is confident enough that a reader could mistake it for a policy finding, and the fact that the Limitations section immediately preceding it concedes the design cannot support causal interpretation makes the contrast sharper.

A NUANCE THE SUMMARY FLATTENS. The Discussion reports that 'Hispanic workers are less likely' to choose strong-linkage majors, citing the pooled Table 2 Column 1 estimate of −.011. But once nativity is interacted (Column 2), the Hispanic main effect flips to +.012 and the Hispanic × Foreign Born term is −.028 — meaning U.S.-born Hispanic workers choose slightly higher-linkage majors than U.S.-born White workers, and the pooled negative is driven entirely by Hispanic immigrants. For a paper whose stated contribution is the race-by-nativity intersection, collapsing that back to an unqualified statement about 'Hispanic workers' in the Discussion undercuts its own point.

STANDING AND WHAT IT SETS UP. Despite the framing problems, this is now plausibly the best available U.S. descriptive evidence on race and nativity heterogeneity in major–occupation alignment returns, largely by default — the question had not been asked with outcome data before. Its durable value is as a benchmark: a set of well-powered, publicly replicable conditional means and associations that later work with better identification will be measured against. The follow-on agenda it opens is clear and the authors name most of it: longitudinal or panel designs with individual fixed effects (NLSY, state administrative data) to handle selection into majors and occupations; institution-level selectivity and academic performance, both absent from the ACS; immigrant-specific factors — legal status, credential recognition, licensure, network access — that would speak to why immigrants who deliberately choose high-linkage majors so consistently fail to reach matched occupations; and, most conspicuously, a decomposition of how much of the racial earnings gap among bachelor's holders alignment actually accounts for, which the paper's abstract effectively promises and its analysis never delivers.

RATING RATIONALE. Adequate rather than strong: the increment over Lu et al. (2024) and Bol et al. (2019) is real but incremental, the novel heterogeneity results are modest in magnitude and never formally tested across groups, the headline framing outruns the analysis in a way that will produce miscitation, and the policy section overreaches. Adequate rather than weak: the contribution is clearly identified and genuinely fills a gap, the execution is careful, the robustness program is more than perfunctory, the Limitations section is honest, and the match-premium and alignment-profile results are solid, well-powered, and reusable.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

This paper sits on unusually favorable ground for verification — free, versioned, DOI-cited IPUMS ACS microdata plus a deposited openICPSR replication package — and it documents its estimating equations, covariate list, fixed effects, weighting, and sample drops more carefully than the field's median. But several first-order construction choices are left underspecified or internally contradictory in the article itself: whether the extract is the pooled 1% annual files or the cited 2013–2017 5-year file, how the linkage score is standardized (which sets the units of every headline coefficient), what rule actually produced the Table A1 matched-occupation crosswalk, and what strata/cluster variables underlie the Taylor-linearized standard errors behind every reported inference. A reader can check the paper's internal arithmetic and its measure ordering from the article alone; reproducing a single coefficient almost certainly requires opening the deposit.

**Strengths:**

- Data are fully public and precisely cited: IPUMS USA v13.0, ACS 2013–2017, with a persistent DOI (10.18128/D010.V13.0). Access requires only free registration — no DUA, no restricted-use application, no institutional gatekeeping. Any reader with a browser can begin a replication today.
- A real replication package is deposited, not promised: the Open Practices Statement points to https://doi.org/10.3886/E249905V1 (openICPSR, version 1) for 'data and analysis files.' Under journal-era norms this deserves substantial credit relative to 'available upon request,' and it is the likely resolution point for most of the ambiguities noted below.
- The novel measures are given formally rather than described loosely: Equation 1 states the mutual-information linkage index with p(j|g) and p(j) defined; Equations 2–3 give the counterfactual-frequency and ratio construction for match; footnote 6 explains precisely how the measure simplifies DiPrete et al. (2017) (education held constant at BA); footnote 8 names the occupation coding scheme (4-digit ACS codes) and links the IPUMS documentation page.
- The paper supplies genuine external check targets that most papers omit. Table A1 publishes the complete 36-major-by-2-occupation matched crosswalk — the full content of the match variable — and Figure A1 publishes the standardized linkage value for all 36 majors. Two cell counts are given in text (librarians N = 4,331; clergy N = 10 within library science), and footnote 9 reports the weighted linkage–match correlation (.275). A replicator can validate the entire measure-construction stage before touching a regression.
- The analytic sample partitions are internally consistent to the individual, which I verified: Table 5's destination Ns sum to 564,888 + 680,344 + 121,371 = 1,366,603, exactly the headline N; and every Table 6 race-by-destination row sums exactly to its Table 3 race total (e.g., White 373,705 + 571,201 + 110,237 = 1,055,143; Asian 77,855 + 34,518 + 2,615 = 114,988). Nothing is silently dropped between tables.
- Sample attrition is documented rather than hidden. Footnote 7 reports the ≥100-observation major threshold and the resulting exclusion (N = 68, all military technologies). Footnotes 10 and 11 explain the small N discrepancies in the logit tables as perfect-prediction state drops, and report that the earnings models were re-estimated on the reduced samples with substantively similar results — exactly the disclosure a replicator needs to reconcile Table 3 against Table 4 and Table 6 against Table 7.
- Robustness work is enumerated and deposited rather than gestured at: regional and Census-division linkage measures (footnote 5; Tables OB1–OB7, OC1–OC7), a 170-category field-of-study specification with 36-field fixed effects (Tables OD1–OD7), and linear probability analogues for every logit (Tables OA1–OA4). AERA Open supplements are open-access, so these are retrievable.
- Specification reporting is complete at the level of the equations: Equations 4–6 are explicit, the covariate list is stated in text and repeated in every table note, state and year fixed effects are named, survey weighting is stated, and N, R², and an F-adjusted goodness-of-fit statistic appear for every model.

**Weaknesses:**

- The extract is described inconsistently, and the two readings are different datasets. The Method section says 'individual-level data from the 1% sample of the ACS spanning the years 2013 to 2017,' while the citation is to the IPUMS 2013–2017 ACS *5-year* sample (Ruggles et al. 2023). These are not the same file: the pooled single-year 1% files and the 5-year (~5%) file differ in size, in weight construction, and in replicate/design variables. Two pieces of internal evidence favor the pooled 1% reading — the reported N of 1,366,603 is roughly what five pooled 1% years yield after the stated restrictions (a 5-year file would give several times more), and the models include *year* fixed effects, which are degenerate in the 5-year file where YEAR is constant and MULTYEAR is required instead. A replicator must resolve this before pulling anything, and the article does not resolve it.
- The standardization of the linkage measure — which fixes the units of every linkage coefficient in Tables 2–7 and the paper's headline '3.9% higher earnings per one-SD increase' claim — is stated only as 'standardized the linkage scores to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1,' without saying whether the standardization runs across the 36 major-level values or across weighted persons. The two produce different scalings and therefore different coefficient magnitudes. Table 1 (All: mean .003, SD 1.008) points to weighted person-level standardization, and the small departure from exactly (0, 1) further implies the standardizing population is the linkage-construction sample, not the analytic sample — but the reader has to reverse-engineer this from summary statistics rather than read it.
- Table A1 contradicts the stated matching rule. The text defines matched occupations as the two with the highest ratio of actual to counterfactual frequency (Eq. 3), but Table A1's column headers read 'Most Common Occupation' and 'Second Most Common Occupation' — a raw-frequency rule. Several entries look like frequency winners rather than ratio winners: ethnic studies and liberal arts both map to 'Secretaries & administrative assistants,' history to 'Secondary school teachers,' and philosophy/religion's second occupation is 'Retail salespersons.' Under a ratio rule, large generic occupations should have ratios near 1 and rarely win. Since match is a core regressor and appears in every interaction the paper interprets, a replicator cannot tell from the article which rule was implemented, or what Table A1 is a check of.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The rows of Table A1 follow the stated ratio rule; the header is the mislabel. In the openICPSR deposit (10.3886/E249905V1), RaceNativityLabor_TabA1.do keeps the top two occupations by an adjusted rank built from the actual-to-counterfactual ratio, and the deposited rank correlates 0.99 with a ratio ranking and 0.27 with raw frequency within majors. The concern that the match variable was built on frequency for low-linkage majors, which would bias Linkage × Match upward, does not hold (moderate confidence: the top-two sets only partly reproduce). Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the ICPSR deposit.

- The standard-error machinery is named but not specified. 'Taylor-linearized variance estimators that account for stratification and clustered correlation' does not say which variables define the strata and clusters — IPUMS supplies STRATA and CLUSTER, but state, household, or major are all plausible alternatives. This matters more than usual here: linkage takes only 36 distinct values assigned to over a million individuals, so whether anything accounts for major-level clustering determines whether the linkage inferences are credible. Every p-value and every significance star in the paper rests on an unstated choice.
- Core variables are never named or defined in IPUMS terms. The earnings variable (INCEARN vs. INCWAGE) is not specified; the deflator used to convert to 2017 dollars is not named; the treatment of ACS top-coded/state-mean-replaced earnings is not mentioned. The race/ethnicity construction is given only as 'self-identify as White, Black, Hispanic, or Asian/Pacific Islander' — the article never states whether Hispanic is assigned via HISPAN regardless of race, whether White/Black/Asian are non-Hispanic, or how many observations were dropped as multiracial, AIAN, or other. (The text also says 'Asian/Pacific Islander' while every table says 'Asian.') Reproducing Table 1's \$71,046 mean requires guessing on at least four of these.
- The unemployment outcome is undefined and sits in apparent tension with the sample definition. The analytic sample is '1,366,603 individuals reporting positive earnings in the survey year,' yet Table 1 reports 1.8–2.8% unemployment. The reconciliation is presumably that ACS earnings cover the prior twelve months while employment status is measured in the reference week — but the paper never says so, never gives the EMPSTAT/LABFORCE coding used, and the line 'For consistency, the unemployment analyses use the same analytic sample as the earnings analyses' makes the reference-period mismatch invisible. Readers should note that the unemployment estimates are identified off people who worked during the year and were out of work at survey time, a narrower and more selected phenomenon than 'unemployment' suggests.
- The population used to *build* the measures differs from the population used to *estimate*, and the paper never states the regression sample's restrictions. Linkage (and the ActualFreq counts behind match) are computed among full-time, non-self-employed, not-in-school, non-armed-forces workers aged 25–64 with a BA as highest degree. The analytic sample is described only as aged 25–64, BA-highest, four race groups, positive earnings — with no full-time or self-employment restriction stated. So part-time and self-employed workers may carry match indicators derived from a distribution that excluded them. This is both a substantive issue and a concrete replication fork that changes N.
- The immigrant-destination rule is not operationalizable as written. 'States receiving over 1% of a specific immigrant group (Mexican, other Latin American, Asian, and other) since the mid-1990s' does not say 1% of what denominator, over which interval, or how 'since the mid-1990s' is computed from the six listed snapshots (1970/1980/1990/2000 censuses plus the 2008–2012 and 2013–2017 ACS), nor how immigrant arrival cohorts are identified. Footnote 4's disclosure of the deviations from Massey and Capoferro (NJ moved to established; AL, NM, OK, SC added; DC included) is welcome, but it documents the *result*, not the rule. The saving grace is that footnote 4 lists all 26 new-destination states explicitly, so the classification is reproducible as a list even though it is not reproducible as a procedure.
- No software environment is reported anywhere — no package, no version, no estimation command. The diagnostics reported ('Taylor-linearized' SEs, an 'F-adjusted goodness-of-fit') strongly suggest Stata's svy suite with the Archer–Lemeshow F-adjusted mean residual test, but this is inference on the reader's part, not documentation.
- The F-adjusted goodness-of-fit statistics are printed without degrees of freedom or p-values, leaving them uninterpretable. Values range from .371 (Table 4, White) to 33.234 and 38.559 (Table 2) to 1987.955 (Table 7, Panel B, Hispanic nondestination). Large values indicate rejection of fit, so several of these appear to signal calibration failure — but the reader cannot tell, and the paper does not comment.
- The Open Practices Statement is a single sentence with no inventory of the deposit: no statement of whether it contains the IPUMS extract itself, an extract-definition file, code only, or all three; no README description, no license, no software or runtime note. A reader deciding whether to attempt replication cannot judge from the article what work the deposit will save them.
- A substantial fraction of the paper's robustness claim structure — roughly 25 supplemental tables across four families — is asserted in the main text as 'substantively similar' or 'substantively unchanged' with no summary of what changed. Footnote 5's regional-linkage check and the 170-category check (whose text does concede 'some estimates differ across specifications') are the two most consequential, and neither is characterized in the article beyond a sentence.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Before pulling any data, open the openICPSR deposit (10.3886/E249905V1) and look first for the extract definition or codebook, then for the linkage/match construction code. Four things you cannot settle from the article should be settled there: whether the extract is the pooled 1% annual files or the 2013–2017 5-year file; whether linkage is standardized across the 36 majors or across weighted persons; whether match uses the ratio rule (Eq. 3) or raw frequency (as Table A1's headers say); and which variables define the survey strata and clusters. If the deposit does not answer these, they are the questions to put to the corresponding author.
- If you must choose without the deposit, the internal evidence favors the pooled single-year 1% files over the cited 5-year file: the reported N of 1,366,603 is the right order of magnitude for five pooled 1% years after the stated restrictions, and year fixed effects require survey-year variation that the 5-year file does not have. Treat this as a working assumption to be confirmed, not as settled.
- Verify the measure-construction stage before any regression — it is the part of the paper most checkable from public sources. Reproduce Figure A1's ordering of the 36 majors (liberal arts, social science, and history at the bottom; electrical/mechanical repairs, cosmetology/culinary arts, and nuclear technologies at the top), and reproduce Table A1's full crosswalk. If your ratio-rule implementation returns distinctive occupations where Table A1 lists generic high-volume ones (ethnic studies and liberal arts to 'Secretaries & administrative assistants'; philosophy/religion's second to 'Retail salespersons'), you have located the rule discrepancy rather than a coding error on your end — resolve it before proceeding, because match drives most of the paper's interpreted interactions.
- Use the two published cell counts as unit tests on the linkage-construction sample: within library science, librarians should number 4,331 and clergy 10. These pin down the sample restrictions (25–64, BA-highest, full-time, not self-employed, not armed forces, not in school) and the weighting convention for the frequency counts more sharply than the prose does.
- Treat the exact magnitude of every linkage coefficient as provisional until the standardization is confirmed. The headline claim that a one-SD increase in linkage is associated with 3.9% higher earnings for matched White workers (and 6.0–6.9% for Black and Hispanic workers) is denominated in an SD whose definition the article does not state. The sign patterns, the ordering across groups, and the Linkage × Match interaction structure are robust to this; the numbers attached to them are not.
- Treat the inference — not the point estimates — as the softest layer of the paper. Linkage varies across only 36 majors but is regressed on 1.37 million individuals, and the paper does not say whether the clustering adjustment addresses that. Before relying on any marginally significant linkage result (the + and * results in Tables 4, 6, and 7 especially), re-estimate with clustering at the major level and see what survives. This is the single check most likely to change how much weight a reader should put on a specific coefficient.
- When reading the unemployment results, hold in mind that the outcome is measured on a positive-earnings sample: these are people who had earnings in the prior twelve months and were not working in the survey reference week. That is a real quantity, but it is not the unemployment rate, and the paper's rates (1.8–2.8%) should not be compared to published BLS figures. Ask the authors for the exact EMPSTAT/LABFORCE coding if you intend to reproduce Table 4.
- Do not attempt to re-derive the immigrant-destination classification from the stated '1% of a specific immigrant group since the mid-1990s' rule — it is not operationalizable from the article. Take footnote 4's 26-state new-destination list, plus CA/FL/NY/TX/IL/NJ as established and the remainder (including DC) as nondestination, as the classification. Because the rule is unreproducible, treat the destination-contrast findings as conditional on the authors' particular partition; a reader who cares about them should check sensitivity to reclassifying the four states the authors added on their own judgment (AL, NM, OK, SC) and to New Jersey's promotion to established.
- Discount the nondestination results independently of any replication concern. Nondestination cells hold only 8.9% of the sample and, for minorities, very few observations (Hispanic N = 2,756; Asian N = 2,615 in Table 6; smaller still in Table 7 after perfect-prediction drops). Table 7's Panel B nondestination columns report an F-adjusted goodness-of-fit of 1987.955 for Hispanics and 25.422 for Asians alongside implausibly extreme odds ratios (.176, 5.942); the authors themselves flag caution here. These cells should not be cited.
- Because the F-adjusted goodness-of-fit statistics are reported without degrees of freedom or p-values, do not read them as evidence of adequate fit. If replicating, recompute them (Stata's estat gof after svy: logit gives the Archer–Lemeshow test) and report the p-value; the Table 2 values of 33.234 and 38.559 and the Table 5 value of 37.387 are large enough to warrant checking whether the match models are in fact rejecting fit.
- What is checkable from the article alone: Table 1's summary statistics (once you fix the extract, the race construction, the earnings variable, and the deflator), Figure A1's linkage ordering, Table A1's crosswalk, the two library-science cell counts, the .275 linkage–match correlation, and the exact internal consistency of sample sizes across Tables 3, 5, and 6 — which I confirmed holds to the person. What is effectively unverifiable without the deposit: every regression coefficient and standard error, the whole robustness apparatus (Tables OA1–OD7), the destination classification rule, and the standardization convention. Weight the paper's descriptive framing accordingly: the patterns it describes are well-documented, the specific magnitudes are conditional on choices the article does not report.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This is a paper whose reproducibility profile is much better than the field median in its raw materials and merely average in its documentation discipline. The materials are close to ideal: public IPUMS ACS microdata behind nothing but a free registration, cited to a versioned DOI; a deposited openICPSR package that the Open Practices Statement names with a resolvable DOI; open-access supplements; and — unusually — the complete content of the paper's two novel measures printed in the appendix, so that Figure A1 and Table A1 together let a replicator validate the entire construction stage before running a single regression. Under the calibration this review is asked to apply, a deposited package earns real credit relative to 'available upon request,' and the authors earned it.

The documentation discipline is where the paper falls to adequate rather than strong. The problems cluster in a recognizable place: everything about the *estimation* is stated (equations, covariates, fixed effects, weighting, N, R²), and a surprising number of things about the *data* are not. The extract is described two different ways in two adjacent sentences — '1% sample' in the text, the 2013–2017 5-year sample in the citation — and these are genuinely different files with different weights and different design variables. The internal evidence resolves it fairly convincingly toward the pooled 1% files (the N is right for that reading, and year fixed effects are degenerate under the other), but a replicator should not have to run that inference. Downstream, the earnings variable is unnamed, the deflator is unnamed, top-coding is unmentioned, the race and Hispanic-origin construction is undefined, and the unemployment measure is undefined in a sample where its presence is at first glance paradoxical. None of these is exotic; all of them are the kind of thing a data-availability statement or a two-paragraph appendix would fix, and their absence means Table 1 — the most basic check target in the paper — cannot be reproduced without a handful of guesses.

Two gaps are more serious than the others because they touch the paper's central quantities rather than its periphery. The first is the standardization of linkage. Everything the paper claims about magnitude is denominated in a standard deviation whose definition is never given: 'standardized to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1' is compatible with standardizing across the 36 major-level values (unweighted, each major counted once) or across weighted persons, and these give different scalings and therefore different coefficients. Table 1's All-column values of mean .003 and SD 1.008 make the weighted person-level reading nearly certain, and the small departure from exactly zero and one is itself informative — it implies the standardizing population is the linkage-construction sample (full-time, non-self-employed, and so on) while the reported summary statistics are computed on the broader analytic sample. That is a useful deduction, but it is a deduction. The headline result that a one-SD increase in linkage is associated with 3.9% higher earnings among matched White workers, rising to 6.0–6.9% for Black and Hispanic workers, cannot be given its stated units by a reader working from the article alone.

The second is Table A1's conflict with the stated matching rule. The text is unambiguous that matched occupations are the top two by the ratio of actual to counterfactual frequency, following Bol et al. (2019). Table A1's headers say 'Most Common Occupation' and 'Second Most Common Occupation,' which is the raw-frequency rule, and several of the entries look like what a frequency rule would produce: ethnic studies and liberal arts both mapping to secretaries and administrative assistants, history to secondary school teachers, philosophy/religion's runner-up being retail salespersons. A ratio rule should push exactly those large, undifferentiated occupations toward ratios near one and out of the top two. Either the headers are mislabeled or the implementation is frequency-based; a replicator cannot tell which from the article, and the answer determines the content of match, which appears in every interaction the paper interprets substantively. This is the single most consequential ambiguity in the paper, and it is unfortunate that it lands on the very artifact that would otherwise be the paper's best verification asset.

*See the correction note in the Methods sub-review above.*

The inference layer is the softest. 'Taylor-linearized variance estimators that account for stratification and clustered correlation' names a method without naming its inputs. IPUMS provides STRATA and CLUSTER, and the phrasing suggests those, but state and household are equally plausible readings, and none of them addresses what a skeptical reader would want addressed: linkage takes 36 distinct values spread over 1.37 million individuals, so the effective number of independent observations on the paper's key regressor is 36, not 1,366,603. Whether anything in the variance estimator reflects that is exactly what the paper does not say. Every star in Tables 2 through 7 depends on the answer. Compounding this, the F-adjusted goodness-of-fit statistics are printed bare — no degrees of freedom, no p-values — so a diagnostic that would let readers judge model calibration is displayed in a form that cannot be read, and several of the values (33.234 and 38.559 in Table 2, 37.387 in Table 5, and an anomalous 1987.955 in Table 7) look large enough to matter.

Against all that, the paper does several transparency things well that deserve to be named, because they are the ones authors most often skip. The sample-drop footnotes are exemplary: footnote 7 reports the exact exclusion (N = 68, military technologies) produced by the ≥100-observation threshold, and footnotes 10 and 11 explain the perfect-prediction state drops in the logit models and report that the earnings models were re-run on the reduced samples with similar results. That is precisely the disclosure that lets a reader reconcile Table 3 with Table 4 without suspecting sample manipulation. And the arithmetic holds: I checked that Table 5's three destination Ns sum exactly to 1,366,603 and that each of Table 6's four race panels sums exactly to its Table 3 race total. Nothing disappears between exhibits.

On robustness, the paper is honest about what it did but thin about what it found. Roughly twenty-five supplemental tables carry the regional and division-level linkage checks, the 170-category field-of-study check with 36-field fixed effects, and linear probability analogues for every logit. These are described almost entirely as 'substantively similar' or 'substantively unchanged.' The 170-category discussion is the one place the paper concedes that 'some estimates differ across specifications' without saying which — for a robustness check specifically motivated as addressing nonrandom major selection, that concession deserves a sentence naming what moved. Readers who care about a particular coefficient should open OD1–OD7 rather than accept the summary.

What this means practically. A reader can independently verify the paper's descriptive architecture — which majors are tightly linked, which occupations count as matched, that the samples partition cleanly, that linkage and match are distinct but correlated at .275 — from the article and public IPUMS alone, with moderate effort and a few documented guesses. A reader cannot verify a single regression coefficient without either the deposit or a willingness to make consequential choices the authors did not report, and cannot verify any of the robustness claims from the article at all. The findings themselves are framed throughout as descriptive associations, and that framing is honest; the reproducibility profile does not undermine the paper's claim structure so much as it means that the specific magnitudes — the 3.9% versus 6.9% contrast that is the paper's most quotable result — should be treated as conditional on unreported choices until the deposit is inspected. My confidence reflects a complete reading of the article, its eleven footnotes, all table notes, and both appendix figures, tempered by the fact that I have not opened the openICPSR package, which very plausibly resolves the extract definition, the standardization convention, the matching rule, and the variance-estimator inputs in a single well-commented script.
